items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which term describes the mental element of a crime?

  1. Actus reus
  2. Mens rea
  3. Causation
  4. Strict liability

Why B: Mens rea is the guilty mind (intention, recklessness or criminal negligence). Actus reus is the physical act.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Why is speeding classed as a strict liability offence?

  1. The prosecution must prove the driver intended to speed
  2. It can only be heard in the District Court
  3. The prosecution only needs to prove the act, not a guilty mind
  4. No penalty can be imposed for it

Why C: Strict liability offences need proof of the actus reus only. An honest and reasonable mistake of fact can still be raised.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Sam punches Lee. Lee falls, hits his head and later dies in hospital from the head injury.

Which element must the prosecution prove to link Sam's punch to Lee's death?

  1. Causation
  2. Motive
  3. Recklessness
  4. Complicity

Why A: Causation requires an unbroken link between the accused's act and the harm.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which statement about summary offences in NSW is correct?

  1. They are heard by a judge and jury in the District Court
  2. They are less serious offences heard by a magistrate in the Local Court
  3. They always begin with a committal hearing
  4. They can only be prosecuted by the Director of Public Prosecutions

Why B: Summary offences are finalised in the Local Court by a magistrate sitting alone, usually with a police prosecutor.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Jo keeps watch at the door while Kim robs a shop.

What is Jo's role in the crime?

  1. Principal in the first degree
  2. Accessory after the fact
  3. Accessory before the fact
  4. Principal in the second degree

Why D: A principal in the second degree is present and assists while the crime is committed. Kim, who commits the act, is the principal in the first degree.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which of the following is an example of situational crime prevention?

  1. A parenting program for young families
  2. Extra funding for school attendance officers
  3. Better street lighting and CCTV at a train station
  4. A youth employment scheme

Why C: Situational prevention makes a crime harder or riskier to commit in a place. The other options are social prevention, which targets the causes of offending.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which Act sets out most police powers in NSW, including search, arrest and detention?

  1. Bail Act 2013 (NSW)
  2. Evidence Act 1995 (NSW)
  3. Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW)
  4. Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999 (NSW)

Why C: The Act, known as LEPRA, brought police powers together in one statute and sets safeguards on their use.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Under the Bail Act 2013 (NSW), what must a bail authority consider for every accused person?

  1. Whether the accused is likely to be found guilty
  2. Whether there is an unacceptable risk that cannot be managed by conditions
  3. Whether the victim agrees to bail
  4. Whether the accused can afford a lawyer

Why B: The unacceptable risk test asks about failing to appear, committing a serious offence, endangering safety and interfering with witnesses or evidence.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which statement best describes the right to silence for a suspect questioned by police in NSW?

  1. A suspect must answer every question once cautioned
  2. A suspect generally need not answer questions, other than giving details such as name and address when required by law
  3. The right applies only to people under 18
  4. The right is lost once a person is arrested

Why B: Police must caution a suspect that they do not have to say or do anything. Some laws require identity details to be given.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which court hears most trials for serious indictable offences such as armed robbery in NSW?

  1. Local Court
  2. District Court
  3. Coroner's Court
  4. Land and Environment Court

Why B: The District Court hears most indictable offences. The Supreme Court hears the most serious, such as murder.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which is a feature of the adversary system?

  1. The judge leads the investigation and questions witnesses
  2. Two opposing sides present their cases before an impartial decision-maker
  3. The accused must prove their innocence
  4. Evidence is collected by the court itself

Why B: In the adversary system the parties run their own cases and the judge or magistrate is an impartial umpire.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is charge negotiation?

  1. The magistrate reducing a sentence after hearing a victim impact statement
  2. An agreement in which the accused pleads guilty in return for a lesser or fewer charges
  3. The jury agreeing on a majority verdict
  4. Police deciding whether to issue a caution

Why B: Charge negotiation takes place between the prosecution and the defence before trial. It saves court time but can be seen as lenient.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is the standard of proof in a criminal trial?

  1. On the balance of probabilities
  2. Beyond reasonable doubt
  3. Reasonable suspicion
  4. A prima facie case

Why B: The prosecution carries the burden and must prove the offence beyond reasonable doubt.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which of the following is a partial defence to murder in NSW?

  1. Self-defence
  2. Duress
  3. Substantial impairment because of mental health impairment or cognitive impairment
  4. Necessity

Why C: A partial defence reduces murder to manslaughter. Self-defence, duress and necessity are complete defences that lead to an acquittal.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
How many jurors usually sit on a criminal trial in NSW, and what verdict can be accepted?

  1. Six jurors; the verdict must be unanimous
  2. Twelve jurors; a majority verdict of 11 to 1 may be accepted after long deliberation
  3. Twelve jurors; a simple majority of 7 to 5 is enough
  4. Four jurors; the verdict must be unanimous

Why B: The Jury Act 1977 (NSW) allows a majority verdict of 11 to 1 when a unanimous verdict cannot be reached after reasonable time.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
A judge says the sentence must "send a message to others who might think of committing this offence". Which purpose of punishment is this?

  1. Specific deterrence
  2. Rehabilitation
  3. General deterrence
  4. Incapacitation

Why C: General deterrence aims to discourage the wider community. Specific deterrence aims at the offender.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which of the following is a mitigating factor in sentencing?

  1. The offence was committed in company
  2. The victim was vulnerable
  3. The offender showed remorse and pleaded guilty early
  4. A weapon was used

Why C: Mitigating factors can reduce a sentence. The other options are aggravating factors under s 21A of the Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999 (NSW).

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which penalty allows an offender to serve a sentence of imprisonment in the community under strict supervision?

  1. Conditional release order
  2. Intensive correction order
  3. Fine
  4. Forfeiture of assets

Why B: An intensive correction order is a custodial sentence served in the community, with conditions such as home detention, curfews or community service.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is parole?

  1. A sentence served entirely in the community
  2. The conditional release of a prisoner to serve the rest of the sentence in the community under supervision
  3. A reduction in sentence for a guilty plea
  4. An order made after a sentence has ended

Why B: Parole helps reintegration under supervision. Breaching conditions can return the offender to custody.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What does doli incapax mean for a child aged 10 to under 14 in NSW?

  1. The child can never be charged with an offence
  2. The child is presumed incapable of criminal intent unless the prosecution proves the child knew the act was seriously wrong
  3. The child must be tried as an adult
  4. The child's parents are criminally responsible

Why B: The presumption can be rebutted. RP v The Queen (2016) confirmed the prosecution must prove the child knew the conduct was seriously wrong in a moral sense.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which options does the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) provide as alternatives to court?

  1. Bail, remand and parole
  2. Warnings, cautions and youth justice conferences
  3. Fines, bonds and control orders
  4. Committal, trial and appeal

Why B: The Act diverts young people from court for less serious offences, in increasing order of seriousness.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which of the following is a transnational crime rather than a crime against the international community?

  1. Genocide
  2. War crimes
  3. Human trafficking across borders
  4. Crimes against humanity

Why C: Transnational crimes cross borders and are prosecuted under domestic law. Genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity can be tried by the International Criminal Court.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is a limitation of the International Criminal Court?

  1. It can only hear civil disputes between countries
  2. It has no police force and relies on states to arrest and surrender suspects
  3. It can only try people under 18
  4. Its decisions must be approved by the High Court of Australia

Why B: The Court depends on state cooperation, and several powerful states are not parties to the Rome Statute.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is circle sentencing?

  1. A sentencing hearing held by three judges
  2. An alternative sentencing court for adult Aboriginal offenders that involves Elders and community members
  3. A program in which prisoners move between prisons
  4. A type of youth justice conference for first offenders

Why B: The magistrate sits with Elders, the offender, and often the victim, to discuss the offence and an appropriate sentence.

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Distinguish between a strict liability offence and an offence that requires mens rea. Use an example of each.

  • Mens rea offences need proof of a guilty mind as well as the act, for example murder or larceny (1)
  • Strict liability offences need proof of the act only, for example speeding (1)
  • Shows the difference clearly, such as what the prosecution must prove (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain how the Bail Act 2013 (NSW) tries to balance the rights of the accused with the safety of the community.

  • Bail lets an accused stay in the community until trial, which respects the presumption of innocence (1)
  • The unacceptable risk test protects the community, victims and witnesses (1)
  • Show cause offences place the onus on the accused for serious charges (1)
  • Conditions such as reporting or curfews can manage risk without remand (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain why access to legal representation is important in a criminal trial. Refer to one case.

  • The adversary system assumes both sides are equally able to present a case (1)
  • An unrepresented accused faces a trained prosecutor and complex rules of evidence (1)
  • Dietrich v The Queen (1992): a trial for a serious offence may be stayed if the accused cannot get representation through no fault of their own (1)
  • Legal Aid NSW applies a means test, a merit test and a jurisdiction test, so some people miss out (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Outline the role of the victim in sentencing.

  • A victim may give a victim impact statement about the harm suffered (1)
  • It is read or given to the court after conviction and before sentence (1)
  • The court may take it into account, but the sentence is still the court's decision (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Describe TWO ways the Children's Court operates differently from an adult court.

  • It is a closed court and the child's name cannot generally be published (2 for a described feature)
  • Proceedings are less formal, and the magistrate must make sure the child understands (2 for a second described feature)

Other acceptable features: a specialist magistrate sits without a jury; rehabilitation is given priority; penalties come from the Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW).

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Assess the effectiveness of ONE domestic or international measure in dealing with international crime.

  • Names a measure, such as the International Criminal Court, extradition treaties or the Australian Federal Police working with Interpol (1)
  • Explains how it works (1)
  • Gives at least one strength with evidence (1)
  • Gives at least one limit, such as state sovereignty, cost or delay (1)
  • Makes a judgement about its effectiveness (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
Police stop Dani, aged 22, outside a shopping centre after a staff member reports that someone matching her description put a phone in her bag without paying. An officer searches her bag without a warrant, finds an unopened phone and arrests her. At the station she is questioned for two hours without being told she does not have to answer.

(a) Identify the power police used to search Dani's bag and what they needed before using it. (2 marks)

  • A search without a warrant under the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW) (1)
  • Police must suspect on reasonable grounds that she has something stolen (1)

(b) Explain whether police acted lawfully at the station. Refer to the scenario. (4 marks)

  • Police must caution a suspect that they do not have to say or do anything (1)
  • Dani was not cautioned, so this safeguard was breached (1)
  • She should also be told of her right to contact a lawyer or support person, and the detention time limits apply (1)
  • A court has a discretion to exclude evidence that was improperly obtained (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
Marco is walking home when a stranger grabs him from behind and threatens him with a broken bottle. Marco pushes the man hard. The man falls, strikes his head on the kerb and is seriously injured. Marco is charged with recklessly causing grievous bodily harm.

(a) Identify the defence Marco is most likely to raise. (1 marks)

Self-defence.

(b) Explain how a court would decide whether the defence succeeds. Refer to the scenario. (4 marks)

  • Marco must have believed his conduct was necessary to defend himself (1)
  • His response must be reasonable in the circumstances as he perceived them (1)
  • A threat with a broken bottle supports both parts of the test (1)
  • Once the defence is raised, the prosecution must disprove it beyond reasonable doubt; if it cannot, Marco is acquitted (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
Tayla, aged 12, is caught spraying paint on a bus shelter. She has never been in trouble with police before. Police take her to the station and want to ask her questions. Her mother is at work and cannot be reached.

(a) Outline how doli incapax applies to Tayla. (2 marks)

  • She is aged 10 to under 14, so she is presumed incapable of criminal intent (1)
  • The prosecution would need to prove she knew the act was seriously wrong (1)

(b) Explain why police should not interview Tayla alone. (2 marks)

  • A child should have a responsible adult present when questioned (1)
  • A statement made without one may not be admitted as evidence (1)

(c) Recommend the most suitable response under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW). Give reasons. (3 marks)

  • A warning or a caution (1)
  • The offence is minor, non-violent and her first (1)
  • Diversion avoids a court record and reduces the risk of reoffending (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
Ravi, aged 34, pleads guilty at the first opportunity to breaking into a house at night while the family was asleep. He stole jewellery worth $4,000. He has two earlier convictions for similar offences. He has since begun treatment for drug addiction and has written a letter of apology to the family.

(a) Identify ONE aggravating factor and ONE mitigating factor in the scenario. (2 marks)

  • Aggravating: prior convictions, or the offence took place in a home at night with the occupants present (1)
  • Mitigating: early guilty plea, remorse or steps towards rehabilitation (1)

(b) Explain which purposes of punishment a court might give most weight to when sentencing Ravi. (4 marks)

  • Names relevant purposes, such as specific deterrence, protection of the community and rehabilitation (1)
  • Links deterrence or protection to his record (1)
  • Links rehabilitation to his treatment (1)
  • Shows the court must balance competing purposes (1)

items.name: Extended response
items.html:
Evaluate the role of discretion in achieving justice in the criminal justice system.

  • Defines discretion and names who uses it: police, prosecutors, magistrates and judges, juries
  • Police discretion: warnings and cautions under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW); decisions to arrest and charge under the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW)
  • Prosecutorial discretion: charge negotiation and the prosecution guidelines
  • Judicial discretion in sentencing: s 21A factors, guideline judgments, and limits such as standard non-parole periods and mandatory sentences
  • Weighs individualised justice against inconsistency and possible bias, using cases, media and reports
  • Makes a sustained judgement

Plan

  • Police: flexibility for minor and young offenders, but uneven use
  • Prosecution and pre-trial: efficiency against transparency
  • Sentencing: individual justice against consistency
  • Judgement: discretion is necessary but needs guidelines and review

items.name: Extended response
items.html:
To what extent does the criminal justice system deal effectively with young offenders?

  • Age of criminal responsibility and doli incapax (RP v The Queen 2016), and the debate about raising the age
  • Rights when questioned and arrested
  • Children's Court procedures and the focus on rehabilitation
  • Diversion under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) and the Youth Koori Court
  • Penalties, detention and reoffending, with statistics from a named source
  • Over-representation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people
  • A judgement that addresses "to what extent"

Plan

  • Different treatment is justified: age and capacity
  • Diversion works for most young people
  • Limits: detention, remand and over-representation
  • Judgement

items.name: Extended response
items.html:
Assess how effectively the criminal trial and sentencing processes balance the rights of victims, offenders and society.

  • Rights of the accused: presumption of innocence, legal representation (Dietrich v The Queen 1992), rules of evidence, appeals
  • Rights of victims: the Charter of Victims Rights, victim impact statements, support services
  • Society: open justice, juries, the purposes of punishment
  • Tensions: charge negotiation, bail, sentencing discounts, mandatory sentences
  • A judgement on the balance, with a range of evidence

Plan

  • Trial: protections for the accused
  • Victims: growing recognition but a limited role
  • Sentencing: community protection against rehabilitation
  • Judgement

items.name: TEEACL paragraph
items.html:
Assess the effectiveness of bail laws in balancing the rights of the accused and the protection of the community.

  • A judgement, for example that the law now favours community protection
  • Evidence: Bail Act 2013 (NSW), the show cause requirement and the unacceptable risk test
  • Analysis against a criterion, such as protection of individual rights or meeting society's needs
  • Counterpoint: the growing remand population and the presumption of innocence
  • A link back to the question

items.name: TEEACL paragraph
items.html:
Evaluate the effectiveness of alternative methods of sentencing in achieving justice.

  • A judgement about circle sentencing or restorative justice
  • Evidence: the program, who takes part and what research from a named source found
  • Analysis against a criterion, such as responsiveness or reducing reoffending
  • Counterpoint: limited places, eligibility rules or mixed results
  • A link back to the question

items.name: Put in order
items.html:
An indictable offence, from arrest to sentence An adult is accused of a serious indictable offence in NSW and pleads not guilty.

  1. Police arrest and charge the suspect
  2. A bail decision is made
  3. The charge is first mentioned in the Local Court
  4. The matter is committed to the District Court for trial
  5. A jury is empanelled
  6. The prosecution and the defence present their evidence
  7. The jury gives its verdict
  8. The judge sentences the offender

items.name: Put in order
items.html:
The order of a criminal trial

  1. The prosecution makes its opening address
  2. Prosecution witnesses give evidence in chief
  3. The defence cross-examines prosecution witnesses
  4. The defence presents its case
  5. Both sides give closing addresses
  6. The judge sums up and directs the jury on the law
  7. The jury retires to consider its verdict

items.html:
Responses to a young offender, from least to most serious

  1. Warning
  2. Caution
  3. Youth justice conference
  4. Children's Court hearing
  5. Control order (detention)

items.name: Cause and effect chain
items.html:
How a crisis can change bail law: A person on bail commits a serious violent offence that is widely reported.

  1. The media report the case and question the bail decision Media coverage shapes public opinion about the law.
  2. The community and victims' groups call for tougher laws Public pressure reaches members of parliament.
  3. The government announces a review or a bill Parliament responds to keep public confidence.
  4. Parliament amends the Bail Act 2013 (NSW) Statute law can change quickly.
  5. More accused people are refused bail The test is harder to meet.
  6. The remand population rises More people who have not been convicted are held in custody.

items.name: Spot the mistake
items.html:
This paragraph answers: "Outline the role of the jury in a criminal trial."

In a criminal trial in the District Court, a jury of six twelve people decides whether the accused is guilty. The jury decides questions of law fact, while the judge decides questions of law. The defence prosecution must prove its case on the balance of probabilities beyond reasonable doubt. If the jury finds the accused guilty, the jury judge decides the sentence.

items.name: Spot the mistake
items.html:
This paragraph answers: "Describe the rights of a suspect who has been arrested in NSW."

Police powers of arrest are set out in the Bail Act 2013 Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW). Before questioning, police must interview caution the suspect, who has a right to silence. A suspect can usually be detained for investigation for up to twenty-four six hours before being charged or released, and a longer period needs a search warrant detention warrant. A suspect is entitled to contact a lawyer.

items.name: Source-based
items.html:
Prison numbers and reoffending (Constructed source for practice. The figures are invented.)

A state report finds that the number of adults in prison has grown faster than the population over ten years. About four in ten adults released from prison return to custody within two years. The report says short prison sentences give little time for treatment programs, while supervised orders served in the community cost far less per day and have lower reoffending rates for comparable offenders.

(a) Outline ONE finding of the report. (2 marks)

  • States a finding accurately (1)
  • Adds detail from the source (1)

(b) Explain what the source suggests about how well imprisonment achieves the purposes of punishment. (4 marks)

  • Imprisonment achieves incapacitation and retribution (1)
  • A high return-to-custody rate suggests weak specific deterrence (1)
  • Short sentences limit rehabilitation (1)
  • Community-based orders may achieve rehabilitation at lower cost (1)

(c) Assess the effectiveness of ONE penalty other than imprisonment. (5 marks)

  • Names a penalty, such as an intensive correction order or a community correction order (1)
  • Explains how it works under the Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999 (NSW) (1)
  • Gives a strength with evidence (1)
  • Gives a limit (1)
  • Makes a judgement (1)

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which level of government makes laws about marriage and divorce in Australia?

  1. The states, under their residual powers
  2. The Commonwealth, under the Constitution
  3. Local councils
  4. The United Nations

Why B: The Constitution gives the Commonwealth power over marriage and divorce. The states keep areas such as adoption and child protection.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is the marriageable age in Australia?

  1. 16 for everyone
  2. 18, or 16 to 17 with a court order in exceptional circumstances
  3. 21
  4. Any age with parental consent

Why B: The Marriage Act 1961 (Cth) sets 18. A person aged 16 or 17 needs a court order and parental consent to marry someone who is 18 or over.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which of the following is NOT a requirement of a valid marriage in Australia?

  1. Both people give real consent
  2. A notice of intended marriage is given at least one month before the wedding
  3. The ceremony is held in a religious building
  4. Two adult witnesses are present

Why C: A marriage can be held anywhere by an authorised celebrant. Consent, notice and witnesses are required.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What must be shown to obtain a divorce in Australia?

  1. That one spouse was at fault
  2. That the marriage has broken down irretrievably, shown by 12 months of separation
  3. That both spouses agree to the divorce
  4. That the couple have no children

Why B: The Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) introduced no-fault divorce. Neither fault nor agreement is needed.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is the paramount consideration when a court makes a parenting order?

  1. The wishes of the parents
  2. The best interests of the child
  3. The income of each parent
  4. An equal split of time

Why B: The Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) makes the child's best interests paramount. There is no rule that time must be equal.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What did the Family Law Amendment Act 2023 (Cth) change about parenting orders?

  1. It removed the best interests test
  2. It removed the presumption of equal shared parental responsibility
  3. It ended family dispute resolution
  4. It moved parenting cases to the Local Court

Why B: From May 2024 the presumption introduced in 2006 no longer applies, and the list of best interests factors was simplified with a stronger focus on safety.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
How does a court divide property after a marriage ends?

  1. Each person keeps what is in their name
  2. Property is always divided equally
  3. The court makes an order that is just and equitable after weighing contributions and future needs
  4. The person who earned more receives everything

Why C: The court counts financial and non-financial contributions, including homemaking and parenting, and each person's future needs.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which statement about an apprehended domestic violence order in NSW is correct?

  1. It is a criminal conviction
  2. It is a civil order, but breaching it is a criminal offence
  3. It can only be applied for by the victim
  4. It lasts for life

Why B: The order is made under the Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 (NSW). Police often apply on the victim's behalf.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which court hears most parenting and property disputes after separation?

  1. The Children's Court of NSW
  2. The Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia
  3. The High Court of Australia
  4. The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal

Why B: The court was formed in 2021. The Children's Court hears care and protection matters under NSW law.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which change gave same-sex couples the right to marry in Australia?

  1. A High Court decision in 2013
  2. A referendum in 2017
  3. An amendment to the Marriage Act 1961 (Cth) in December 2017
  4. A treaty ratified in 2009

Why C: Parliament changed the definition of marriage to "the union of 2 people" after the postal survey. It was a survey, not a referendum.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which statement about surrogacy in NSW is correct?

  1. Commercial surrogacy is legal if it is arranged overseas
  2. Only altruistic surrogacy is permitted
  3. The intended parents are the legal parents from birth
  4. Surrogacy agreements are enforced by the courts

Why B: The Surrogacy Act 2010 (NSW) bans commercial surrogacy, including overseas arrangements by NSW residents. Parentage is transferred by a court order.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which Act allows a child at risk of significant harm to be removed from the family home in NSW?

  1. Family Law Act 1975 (Cth)
  2. Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998 (NSW)
  3. Adoption Act 2000 (NSW)
  4. Marriage Act 1961 (Cth)

Why B: The Act governs reports, investigations and care orders made by the Children's Court.

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain how the law recognises de facto relationships.

  • A de facto couple live together on a genuine domestic basis (1)
  • Courts look at factors such as how long they have lived together and shared finances (1)
  • Since 2009 the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) has covered property and maintenance for most de facto couples (1)
  • Children are treated the same whether or not their parents are married (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain why the law encourages families to resolve disputes without going to court.

  • Family dispute resolution is usually required before applying for a parenting order (1)
  • It is cheaper and faster than a hearing (1)
  • Agreements parents make themselves are more likely to last (1)
  • It reduces conflict that harms children (1)
  • A limit: it is not suitable where there is family violence or an imbalance of power (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
Priya and Tom married eight years ago and have a daughter, Mia, aged 6. They separated ten months ago but still live in the same house because neither can afford to move out. Tom wants a divorce now. Priya wants Mia to live mainly with her.

(a) Explain whether Tom can apply for a divorce now. (3 marks)

  • The ground is irretrievable breakdown, shown by 12 months of separation (1)
  • Only ten months have passed, so he must wait (1)
  • Separation under one roof can count, but it must be proved (1)

(b) Explain how a decision about Mia's living arrangements would be made if Priya and Tom cannot agree. (4 marks)

  • They must usually try family dispute resolution first (1)
  • A court can then make a parenting order (1)
  • Mia's best interests are the paramount consideration (1)
  • The court considers her safety, her views and her need for a relationship with both parents where that is safe (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
Over two years, Jordan's partner has checked Jordan's phone every day, controlled all the money, and stopped Jordan from seeing friends. Last week the partner threatened to hurt Jordan if Jordan left. Jordan lives in NSW and is frightened.

(a) Identify TWO legal protections available to Jordan. (2 marks)

  • An apprehended domestic violence order (1)
  • Criminal charges, such as for intimidation or coercive control (1)

(b) Assess how effective these protections are likely to be. (4 marks)

  • An order sets clear conditions and police can apply for it (1)
  • A breach is a criminal offence (1)
  • Limits: orders are sometimes breached and victims may fear reporting (1)
  • A judgement, with reference to support services or recent reform (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
Elena and Chris were married for 15 years. Chris worked full time and paid the mortgage. Elena left paid work to care for their three children and now earns much less than Chris. The house is in Chris's name only. They have separated and cannot agree on how to divide their property.

(a) Outline TWO types of contribution a court would consider. (2 marks)

  • Financial contributions, such as income and mortgage payments (1)
  • Non-financial contributions, such as homemaking and caring for children (1)

(b) Explain why Elena could receive a share of the house even though it is in Chris's name. (4 marks)

  • The court looks at all the property of both people, whoever holds title (1)
  • Her contributions as homemaker and parent are recognised (1)
  • Future needs matter: her lower earning capacity and care of the children (1)
  • The order must be just and equitable in all the circumstances (1)

items.name: Extended response
items.html:
To what extent has family law responded to changing community values?

  • The changing concept of family
  • No-fault divorce under the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth)
  • Recognition of de facto and same-sex relationships, including the 2017 change to the Marriage Act 1961 (Cth)
  • Parental responsibility: the 2006 and 2023 reforms
  • Surrogacy and birth technologies
  • Domestic violence: recognition of coercive control
  • Areas where the law lags, with media and reports as evidence
  • A sustained judgement on extent

Plan

  • Relationships: the law caught up slowly, then decisively
  • Children: from parents' rights to children's safety
  • New technology: the law trails practice
  • Violence: values changed first, the law followed
  • Judgement

items.name: Extended response
items.html:
Evaluate the effectiveness of legal and non-legal responses in protecting family members from harm.

  • Domestic violence: apprehended domestic violence orders, police powers, the coercive control offence
  • Children: mandatory reporting, the Children's Court, out-of-home care
  • Family Law Act 1975 (Cth): safety in parenting decisions
  • Non-legal responses: refuges, helplines, non-government organisations and the media
  • Limits: under-reporting, breaches, resources, remote communities
  • A judgement using criteria such as enforceability, accessibility and protection of rights

Plan

  • Legal responses to domestic violence
  • Care and protection of children
  • Non-legal responses fill gaps
  • Judgement

items.name: TEEACL paragraph
items.html:
Assess the effectiveness of law reform in protecting the best interests of children after separation.

  • A judgement about the 2023 reforms
  • Evidence: Family Law Amendment Act 2023 (Cth) and what it removed
  • Analysis against protection of rights or responsiveness
  • Counterpoint: cost and delay in the courts remain
  • A link back to the question

Resolving a parenting dispute after separation

  1. The parents separate
  2. The parents try to agree between themselves, perhaps in a parenting plan
  3. The parents attend family dispute resolution
  4. A certificate is issued if no agreement is reached
  5. One parent applies to the court for a parenting order
  6. The court considers the best interests of the child
  7. The court makes a parenting order

items.name: Spot the mistake
items.html:
This paragraph answers: "Outline the law on divorce in Australia."

Divorce is governed by the Marriage Act 1961 Family Law Act 1975 (Cth). The only ground is that the marriage has broken down irretrievably, shown by six 12 months of separation. The court must does not consider who was at fault. If there are children under 18, the court must be satisfied that the parents have equal time proper arrangements have been made for their care.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which word describes human rights as belonging to all people everywhere?

  1. Inalienable
  2. Universal
  3. Indivisible
  4. Collective

Why B: Universal means the rights apply to everyone. Inalienable means they cannot be taken away.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Why is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights described as soft law?

  1. It applies only to developed countries
  2. It is a declaration that is not legally binding on states
  3. It was replaced by the United Nations Charter
  4. It can be enforced by the International Criminal Court

Why B: A declaration states principles. It has great moral force and inspired binding treaties such as the two 1966 covenants.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which of the following is a collective right?

  1. The right to a fair trial
  2. The right to vote
  3. The right to self-determination
  4. The right to freedom of religion

Why C: Self-determination belongs to a people as a group. The other options are individual civil and political rights.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
How can state sovereignty limit the protection of human rights?

  1. States must obey every resolution of the General Assembly
  2. A state can refuse to ratify a treaty or to let outside bodies review its conduct
  3. Sovereign states cannot make their own laws
  4. Sovereignty lets individuals sue their government in any court

Why B: International law depends largely on consent. A state can decline to sign, ratify or comply.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which United Nations body can authorise binding measures such as sanctions?

  1. The General Assembly
  2. The Human Rights Council
  3. The Security Council
  4. The International Court of Justice

Why C: Security Council resolutions can bind member states, but any of the five permanent members can veto them.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which statement about the International Court of Justice is correct?

  1. It tries individuals for war crimes
  2. It hears disputes between states that accept its jurisdiction
  3. It hears complaints from individuals against their own government
  4. It is part of the Australian court hierarchy

Why B: Only states can be parties before the Court. Individuals are tried by the International Criminal Court.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Australia has a dualist system. What does this mean for a human rights treaty that Australia has ratified?

  1. It becomes part of Australian law at once
  2. It has no effect in domestic law until parliament passes legislation to give it effect
  3. It overrides the Constitution
  4. It applies only in the territories

Why B: Parliament must enact a treaty, as it did in part with the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth).

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which right is expressly protected by the Australian Constitution?

  1. Freedom of speech
  2. The right to privacy
  3. Freedom of religion, in s 116
  4. The right to housing

Why C: Section 116 stops the Commonwealth making laws to establish a religion or prohibit its free exercise. Freedom of political communication is implied, not express.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which is an argument against a national Charter of Rights for Australia?

  1. It would educate people about their rights
  2. It would bring Australia into line with other democracies
  3. It could shift power from elected parliaments to unelected judges
  4. It would protect minorities

Why C: Opponents say rights are already protected by parliament, the common law and the Constitution, and that a charter could give judges too much power.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which of the following is a non-government organisation that promotes human rights?

  1. The United Nations Human Rights Council
  2. Amnesty International
  3. The High Court of Australia
  4. The Australian Human Rights Commission

Why B: Amnesty International is independent of government. It investigates and reports on abuses and campaigns for change.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which case is an example of the High Court finding an implied freedom in the Constitution?

  1. Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992)
  2. Dietrich v The Queen (1992)
  3. Australian Capital Television v Commonwealth (1992)
  4. Donoghue v Stevenson (1932)

Why C: The Court held that the system of representative government in the Constitution implies a freedom of political communication.

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Outline how recognition of ONE human right has developed over time.

  • Names a right, such as freedom from slavery, universal suffrage or universal education (1)
  • Describes an early stage, such as a campaign or a national law (1)
  • Describes later international recognition, such as an article of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain the role of the United Nations in promoting and enforcing human rights.

  • The General Assembly adopts declarations and treaties (1)
  • The Human Rights Council reviews each state's record (1)
  • The Security Council can impose sanctions or authorise intervention (1)
  • Treaty committees monitor compliance with reports (1)
  • A limit, such as the veto or reliance on state consent (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Compare the protection of human rights by statute law and by common law in Australia.

  • Statute: parliament enacts specific protections, such as the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) (1)
  • Statute can be changed or repealed by a later parliament (1)
  • Common law: judges recognise rights case by case, such as the right to a fair trial in Dietrich v The Queen (1992) (1)
  • Common law can be overridden by clear legislation (1)
  • A similarity (1)
  • A difference stated clearly (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Evaluate the effectiveness of legal responses to ONE contemporary human rights issue.

  • Names and outlines the issue (1)
  • International legal responses, with a named instrument (1 to 2)
  • Domestic legal responses, with named legislation or a case (1 to 2)
  • Limits, such as sovereignty or enforcement (1)
  • A reasoned judgement (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
Amira applies for a job as a sales assistant. The manager tells her she interviewed well but that customers "would not be comfortable" with her headscarf, and gives the job to someone else. Amira wants to know what she can do.

(a) Identify the type of law that protects Amira and ONE body she could complain to. (2 marks)

  • Anti-discrimination legislation, such as the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth) or the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW) (1)
  • The Australian Human Rights Commission or Anti-Discrimination NSW (1)

(b) Explain how her complaint would be dealt with and what might limit the outcome. (4 marks)

  • The body investigates and tries to conciliate the complaint (1)
  • If conciliation fails she can take the matter to a court or tribunal (1)
  • Remedies can include an apology or compensation (1)
  • Limits include cost, time, proof and gaps in the grounds each Act covers (1)

items.name: TEEACL paragraph
items.html:
To what extent does state sovereignty limit the protection of human rights?

  • A judgement about extent
  • Evidence: a named treaty or body and a named example of a state refusing to comply
  • Analysis against enforceability
  • Counterpoint: sovereignty is also how rights become domestic law
  • A link back to the question

items.name: Spot the mistake
items.html:
This paragraph answers: "Outline how human rights are formally recognised."

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in 1966 1948 by the United Nations Security Council General Assembly. It is a binding treaty non-binding declaration. In 1966 two covenants turned many of its rights into treaty obligations. Because Australia is a monist dualist state, these treaties only become part of domestic law when parliament enacts them.

items.name: Put in order
items.html:
How a human rights treaty becomes Australian law

  1. States negotiate the text of the treaty
  2. The treaty is adopted and opened for signature
  3. Australia signs the treaty
  4. The treaty is tabled in parliament and reviewed by a committee
  5. Australia ratifies the treaty
  6. Parliament passes legislation to give the treaty effect in domestic law

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which international instrument recognises a right to adequate housing as part of an adequate standard of living?

  1. International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
  2. International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
  3. Rome Statute
  4. Refugee Convention

Why B: Article 11 of the Covenant covers an adequate standard of living, including housing. Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights says the same.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which system of land registration is used for most land in NSW?

  1. Old system title
  2. Torrens title
  3. Native title
  4. Company title

Why B: Torrens title, under the Real Property Act 1900 (NSW), relies on a central register guaranteed by the state.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
A buyer purchases a house at auction in NSW. Which statement is correct?

  1. The buyer has a five business day cooling-off period
  2. The buyer has no cooling-off period
  3. The buyer can withdraw at any time before settlement
  4. The seller can accept a higher offer after the auction

Why B: The cooling-off period applies to private treaty sales only. An auction sale is binding when the hammer falls.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What does a buyer forfeit if they withdraw from a private treaty purchase during the cooling-off period in NSW?

  1. Nothing
  2. 0.25 per cent of the purchase price
  3. The full 10 per cent deposit
  4. The cost of the seller's legal fees

Why B: The Conveyancing Act 1919 (NSW) lets the buyer withdraw but the seller keeps 0.25 per cent of the price.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is the maximum rental bond a landlord can ask for in NSW?

  1. Two weeks' rent
  2. Four weeks' rent
  3. Eight weeks' rent
  4. Any amount the tenant agrees to

Why B: The Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW) caps the bond at four weeks' rent. It must be lodged with NSW Fair Trading.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which of the following is an obligation of a landlord under a residential tenancy agreement?

  1. To pay the tenant's electricity bills
  2. To keep the premises in a reasonable state of repair
  3. To inspect the premises every week
  4. To approve the tenant's guests

Why B: The landlord must provide premises that are fit to live in and keep them in reasonable repair. Entry is limited and needs notice.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What changed for NSW tenants in May 2025?

  1. Rental bonds were abolished
  2. Landlords could no longer end a tenancy without giving a reason set out in the law
  3. Rent increases were banned
  4. Tenancy disputes moved to the District Court

Why B: Amendments to the Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW) ended "no grounds" evictions for both periodic and fixed-term leases.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Where would a tenant in NSW go to dispute a landlord's claim on their bond?

  1. The Local Court
  2. The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal
  3. The Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia
  4. The Land and Environment Court

Why B: The Tribunal hears tenancy disputes cheaply and with little formality. Parties usually represent themselves.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which is an example of alternative dispute resolution for neighbours arguing about a fence?

  1. A trial in the District Court
  2. Mediation at a Community Justice Centre
  3. A complaint to the High Court
  4. A police caution

Why B: Community Justice Centres offer free mediation in NSW. The neighbours keep control of the outcome.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
A landlord refuses to rent a flat to a woman because she has young children. Which NSW Act is most relevant?

  1. Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW)
  2. Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW)
  3. Real Property Act 1900 (NSW)
  4. Conveyancing Act 1919 (NSW)

Why B: The Act makes discrimination in accommodation unlawful on grounds that include sex, race, disability and responsibilities as a carer.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which statement about homelessness in Australia is correct?

  1. Most people counted as homeless are sleeping rough
  2. People in severely crowded dwellings and temporary accommodation are counted as homeless
  3. Homelessness affects only adults
  4. Homelessness is a criminal offence

Why B: The Australian Bureau of Statistics counts several groups. People sleeping rough are a small share of the total.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is the main purpose of social housing?

  1. To give investors a tax deduction
  2. To provide secure, affordable rental housing for people on low incomes who cannot afford the private market
  3. To help first home buyers save a deposit
  4. To house tourists

Why B: Social housing includes public, community and Aboriginal housing. Rent is usually set as a share of income.

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain how the law protects a person buying a home in NSW.

  • The seller must disclose documents in the contract for sale, such as the title search and the zoning certificate (1)
  • A cooling-off period applies to private treaty sales (1)
  • Torrens title guarantees the registered title (1)
  • Building and pest inspections are still the buyer's job: caveat emptor (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain the rights and obligations of tenants under the Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW).

  • Right to quiet enjoyment and to premises that are fit to live in (1)
  • Right to have urgent repairs done (1)
  • Limits on bonds, rent increases and landlord entry (1)
  • Obligation to pay rent on time and keep the premises reasonably clean (1)
  • Obligation not to cause damage or a nuisance (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Assess the effectiveness of government responses to housing affordability.

  • Describes the problem with a statistic from a named source (1)
  • A response for buyers, such as stamp duty concessions or deposit guarantees (1)
  • A response for renters, such as Commonwealth Rent Assistance or tenancy reform (1)
  • A supply response, such as planning reform or housing targets (1)
  • A limit, such as demand-side measures pushing prices up (1)
  • A judgement (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
Mei rents a flat in Sydney on a 12-month lease. In month four the hot water system breaks. She emails the agent three times over two weeks and nothing happens. She pays a plumber $900 to fix it and asks the landlord to repay her. The landlord refuses and says she will be evicted for "causing trouble".

(a) Identify the landlord's obligation that has been breached. (2 marks)

  • To keep the premises in reasonable repair (1)
  • A failed hot water service is an urgent repair (1)

(b) Explain whether Mei can recover the $900. (3 marks)

  • A tenant can arrange urgent repairs if the landlord cannot be contacted or does not act (1)
  • The landlord must repay reasonable costs up to the limit set by the regulations (1)
  • She should keep her notices and receipts as evidence (1)

(c) Explain how the dispute could be resolved and whether the landlord's threat is lawful. (3 marks)

  • She can apply to the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal for an order (1)
  • The Tribunal can refuse to end a tenancy where the landlord's notice is retaliatory (1)
  • A landlord now needs a ground set out in the Act to end a tenancy (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
Sam and Alex find a house they love. The agent says another buyer is interested and urges them to sign today. They exchange contracts by private treaty on Monday and pay a deposit. On Wednesday a building inspector finds serious termite damage.

(a) Outline what the cooling-off period allows Sam and Alex to do. (2 marks)

  • Withdraw from the contract within five business days of exchange (1)
  • They forfeit 0.25 per cent of the price (1)

(b) Explain how the outcome would differ if they had bought the house at auction. (3 marks)

  • No cooling-off period applies at auction (1)
  • They would be bound to complete or lose their deposit (1)
  • Inspections must be done before bidding (1)

(c) Explain what caveat emptor means for buyers. (2 marks)

  • The buyer bears the risk of defects they could have found (1)
  • Buyers should get building, pest and strata reports before they commit (1)

items.name: Extended response
items.html:
Evaluate the effectiveness of the law in protecting the rights of tenants.

  • Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW): bonds, repairs, rent increases, entry
  • The 2025 reforms: the end of no-grounds evictions and rules on pets
  • The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal: cheap and fast, but tenants often do not use it
  • Boarders and lodgers: weaker protection
  • Discrimination and affordability as limits on rights in practice
  • Non-legal responses: the Tenants' Union, tenant advice services, the media
  • A judgement using criteria such as accessibility, enforceability and responsiveness

Plan

  • The rights on paper
  • Enforcement through the Tribunal
  • Reform: security of tenure
  • Gaps: marginal renters and affordability
  • Judgement

items.name: Extended response
items.html:
Assess the role of the law in responding to homelessness.

  • The right to shelter in international law, and the lack of an enforceable right in Australia
  • Causes of homelessness: family violence, affordability, health
  • Legal responses: social housing, funding agreements between governments, tenancy protections
  • Non-legal responses: specialist homelessness services and charities
  • Limits: waiting lists, funding and supply
  • A judgement with statistics from a named source

Plan

  • The scale of the problem and the right
  • Legal responses
  • Non-legal responses carry much of the load
  • Judgement

items.name: TEEACL paragraph
items.html:
Assess the effectiveness of the law in dealing with discrimination in housing.

  • A judgement
  • Evidence: Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW) and the complaint process
  • Analysis against enforceability: discrimination is hard to prove
  • Counterpoint: complaints can be conciliated cheaply
  • A link back to the question

items.name: Put in order
items.html:
Buying a home by private treaty in NSW

  1. The buyer arranges loan pre-approval
  2. The buyer inspects the property and makes an offer
  3. The seller's agent sends the contract for sale to the buyer's conveyancer
  4. Contracts are exchanged and the deposit is paid
  5. The cooling-off period runs
  6. The lender finalises the mortgage
  7. Settlement takes place and the balance is paid
  8. The transfer is registered and the buyer becomes the registered owner

items.name: Spot the mistake
items.html:
This paragraph answers: "Outline how a tenancy begins and how disputes are resolved in NSW."

A tenancy in NSW is governed by the Real Property Act 1900 Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW). The tenant pays a bond of up to eight four weeks' rent, which must be lodged with the landlord's bank NSW Fair Trading. Both sides sign a title deed condition report that records the state of the property. If a dispute cannot be settled, either side can apply to the District Court NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which of the following is a reason for law reform?

  1. Laws should never change
  2. Changing social values, new technology and the failure of existing law
  3. Judges prefer new laws
  4. The Constitution requires a new law every year

Why B: Law must keep up with society. When it falls behind, people lose confidence in it.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Laws on cyberbullying and image-based abuse were introduced mainly in response to which driver?

  1. International treaties on trade
  2. New technology
  3. A change to the Constitution
  4. The cost of running the courts

Why B: Existing laws did not cover new kinds of harm made possible by smartphones and social media.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which is a formal method of driving law reform?

  1. A protest march
  2. A social media campaign
  3. A report by a law reform commission
  4. A newspaper editorial

Why C: Law reform commissions and royal commissions are set up by governments to inquire and recommend. Protests, campaigns and the media are informal methods.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What can a law reform commission do?

  1. Pass new laws
  2. Strike down invalid laws
  3. Research an area of law and recommend changes to the government
  4. Sentence offenders

Why C: Commissions advise. Only parliament can enact their recommendations, and it does not have to.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
How can courts change the law?

  1. By holding a referendum
  2. By interpreting statutes and creating precedents in the cases that come before them
  3. By introducing bills into parliament
  4. By giving royal assent

Why B: Judges make law only when a case raises the issue. Parliament can override a decision by passing a statute.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which is a limitation of law reform through parliament?

  1. Parliament cannot change statute law
  2. Reform can be slow and shaped by political interests
  3. Parliament can only act when a case is brought
  4. Acts of parliament apply to one person only

Why B: Governments may avoid controversial reforms or lack the numbers to pass them. Courts, not parliament, must wait for a case.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What did the High Court decide in Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992)?

  1. That terra nullius applied to Australia
  2. That native title exists at common law where traditional connection to the land has continued
  3. That all freehold land must be returned
  4. That the Constitution recognises Aboriginal sovereignty

Why B: The Court rejected terra nullius and recognised the native title of the Meriam people to the Murray Islands.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which Act did the Commonwealth Parliament pass in response to the Mabo decision?

  1. Aboriginal Land Rights Act 1983 (NSW)
  2. Native Title Act 1993 (Cth)
  3. Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth)
  4. Marriage Act 1961 (Cth)

Why B: The Act set up a process for claiming native title and the National Native Title Tribunal.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
How do land rights under the Aboriginal Land Rights Act 1983 (NSW) differ from native title?

  1. Land rights are granted by statute and do not need proof of continuous traditional connection
  2. Land rights come from the common law
  3. Land rights apply only in the Torres Strait
  4. There is no difference

Why A: Land councils can claim certain unused Crown land as compensation for dispossession. Native title recognises rights that have survived under traditional law and custom.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What does the Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act 2024 (Cth) require?

  1. Parents must supervise all internet use
  2. Age-restricted social media platforms must take reasonable steps to prevent people under 16 from having accounts
  3. Children under 16 who use social media are fined
  4. Schools must ban mobile phones

Why B: The duty is on the platforms, not on children or parents. The rules took effect on 10 December 2025.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Who enforces the social media minimum age law?

  1. The NSW Police Force
  2. The eSafety Commissioner
  3. The High Court
  4. The Australian Human Rights Commission

Why B: The eSafety Commissioner oversees compliance. Platforms that fail to take reasonable steps face large civil penalties.

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain how the media can drive law reform.

  • The media report on problems and individual cases (1)
  • Coverage shapes public opinion (1)
  • Public pressure reaches politicians, who respond to keep support (1)
  • An example of a law changed after a media campaign (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain how the Mabo decision led to changes in the law.

  • The High Court rejected terra nullius in 1992 (1)
  • It recognised native title at common law (1)
  • The decision created uncertainty about land claims (1)
  • Parliament responded with the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth) (1)
  • The case shows courts and parliament both making law (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Assess the benefits and limitations of the social media minimum age law as an example of law reform.

  • Outlines the reform (1)
  • A benefit, such as protecting young people from online harm (1)
  • A second benefit, such as placing responsibility on platforms (1)
  • A limitation, such as difficulty verifying age or privacy concerns (1)
  • A second limitation, such as young people moving to less regulated services or losing connection (1)
  • A judgement (1)

items.name: Cause and effect chain
items.html:
From concern to law: the social media minimum age: Parents, researchers and the media raise concerns about the effect of social media on young people's mental health.

  1. Advocacy groups and media campaigns call for an age limit Informal methods build public pressure.
  2. Governments announce support for a minimum age Political will is needed before parliament acts.
  3. A bill is introduced into the Commonwealth Parliament Statute law is the fastest way to regulate a new problem.
  4. Parliament passes the Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act 2024 (Cth) Both houses agreed to the bill.
  5. The eSafety Commissioner prepares to enforce the law An independent regulator is given the job.
  6. Platforms must take reasonable steps to keep under-16s from holding accounts The duty began on 10 December 2025.

items.name: Cause and effect chain
items.html:
From the Murray Islands to the Native Title Act: In 1982 Eddie Koiki Mabo and other Meriam people begin a legal claim to their traditional lands.

  1. The case reaches the High Court Only the High Court could overturn the doctrine of terra nullius.
  2. The High Court rejects terra nullius in 1992 The Court found the doctrine was wrong in fact and unjust.
  3. Native title is recognised at common law Traditional rights survived where connection continued and had not been extinguished.
  4. Governments, miners and farmers seek certainty No one knew which land could be claimed.
  5. Parliament passes the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth) Statute set up a process for claims.

items.name: Put in order
items.html:
How a law reform commission inquiry leads to a new law

  1. The Attorney-General gives the commission terms of reference
  2. The commission researches the law and releases a discussion paper
  3. The public and experts make submissions
  4. The commission gives its final report with recommendations
  5. The government decides which recommendations to accept
  6. A bill is introduced and passed by parliament

items.name: Spot the mistake
items.html:
This paragraph answers: "Outline the significance of the Mabo decision."

In 1982 1992 the Supreme Court of Queensland High Court of Australia decided Mabo v Queensland (No 2). The Court confirmed rejected the doctrine of terra nullius and recognised land rights native title at common law. The next year parliament passed the Aboriginal Land Rights Act Native Title Act 1993 (Cth).

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Who brings a criminal case to court?

  1. The victim
  2. The state, through the police or the Director of Public Prosecutions
  3. The plaintiff
  4. The jury

Why B: A crime is treated as a wrong against the whole community, so the state prosecutes.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What must the prosecution prove for most criminal offences?

  1. Motive and opportunity
  2. Actus reus and mens rea
  3. Breach and loss
  4. Offer and acceptance

Why B: The physical act and the guilty mind must both be proved. Strict liability offences are the exception.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
A driver is fined for travelling 15 km/h over the speed limit. She says she did not notice the sign.

Why is she still liable?

  1. Speeding is an indictable offence
  2. Speeding is a strict liability offence, so intention need not be proved
  3. She has the burden of proving her innocence beyond reasonable doubt
  4. Driving offences are civil matters

Why B: For strict liability offences the prosecution proves the act only.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is the standard of proof in a civil case?

  1. Beyond reasonable doubt
  2. On the balance of probabilities
  3. Beyond any doubt
  4. Reasonable suspicion

Why B: The plaintiff must show their version is more likely than not.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which case established the modern law of negligence and the "neighbour principle"?

  1. Mabo v Queensland (No 2)
  2. Donoghue v Stevenson
  3. Dietrich v The Queen
  4. RP v The Queen

Why B: In 1932 the House of Lords held that a manufacturer owed a duty of care to the person who consumed its product.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What must a plaintiff prove to succeed in a negligence claim?

  1. Intention, act and motive
  2. A duty of care, a breach of that duty, and damage caused by the breach
  3. Offer, acceptance and consideration
  4. Guilt beyond reasonable doubt

Why B: These are the elements of negligence. Offer, acceptance and consideration are elements of a contract.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which of the following is needed for a valid contract?

  1. A written document signed in front of a witness
  2. Offer, acceptance, consideration and an intention to create legal relations
  3. Approval by a court
  4. Payment in full in advance

Why B: Many contracts are verbal. The elements, not the form, make an agreement binding.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is the most common remedy in a civil case?

  1. Imprisonment
  2. A fine paid to the state
  3. Damages paid to the plaintiff
  4. A community correction order

Why C: Civil remedies aim to compensate the person who was wronged. Fines and imprisonment are criminal sanctions.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
A person wants an independent body to take a fresh look at a Commonwealth visa decision and, if it is wrong, change it. Which process is this?

  1. Judicial review
  2. Merits review
  3. A criminal appeal
  4. A referendum

Why B: Merits review, by a body such as the Administrative Review Tribunal, reconsiders the facts, law and policy. Judicial review only asks whether the decision was lawful.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which body investigates complaints about the conduct of NSW government agencies?

  1. The NSW Ombudsman
  2. The Director of Public Prosecutions
  3. The Coroner's Court
  4. The Law Society of NSW

Why A: The Ombudsman is independent, free to use and can recommend changes, but cannot usually force an agency to act.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which is an advantage of using a tribunal rather than a court?

  1. Tribunals can impose prison sentences
  2. Tribunals are usually cheaper, quicker and less formal
  3. Tribunal decisions can never be appealed
  4. Tribunals always use juries

Why B: Tribunals such as the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal are designed to be accessible to people without lawyers.

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Distinguish between criminal law and civil law.

  • Purpose: criminal law punishes and protects the community; civil law compensates (1)
  • Parties: the state against an accused; a plaintiff against a defendant (1)
  • Standard of proof: beyond reasonable doubt; balance of probabilities (1)
  • Outcome: guilty and a sanction; liable and a remedy (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain TWO ways a person can challenge a decision made by a government agency.

  • Names and explains one way, such as internal review, merits review by a tribunal, a complaint to the Ombudsman or judicial review by a court (2)
  • Names and explains a second way (2)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Assess the effectiveness of alternative dispute resolution in resolving civil disputes.

  • Describes a method, such as mediation (1)
  • Strengths: lower cost, speed and privacy (1)
  • The parties keep control and relationships are preserved (1)
  • Limits: an imbalance of power, no binding precedent, and the need for cooperation (1)
  • A judgement (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
Ben buys a takeaway salad from a cafe. Halfway through eating it he finds a piece of broken glass and cuts his mouth. He needs stitches and misses three days of work. The cafe owner says a jar broke in the kitchen that morning and the staff "thought they had cleaned it all up".

(a) Explain whether the cafe owed Ben a duty of care and whether it was breached. (3 marks)

  • A business that sells food owes a duty of care to its customers (1)
  • Harm from glass in food is reasonably foreseeable (1)
  • Serving food after a jar broke nearby, without proper checks, is a failure to take reasonable care (1)

(b) Identify the remedy Ben would seek and what it would cover. (2 marks)

  • Damages (1)
  • Medical costs, lost wages, and pain and suffering (1)

(c) Explain why Ben's case is a civil matter and not a criminal one. (2 marks)

  • It is a dispute between private parties about compensation (1)
  • Ben, as plaintiff, must prove his case on the balance of probabilities (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
Lina's application for a disability support payment is refused by a Commonwealth agency. The letter gives no clear reasons. She believes the officer ignored her doctor's report.

(a) Outline the first steps Lina should take. (2 marks)

  • Ask the agency for reasons and for an internal review (1)
  • Keep to the time limits for review (1)

(b) Explain how a tribunal could help if the internal review fails. (3 marks)

  • The Administrative Review Tribunal can conduct a merits review (1)
  • It looks at the evidence afresh, including the doctor's report (1)
  • It can affirm, vary or set aside the decision (1)

items.name: Put in order
items.html:
Steps in a civil dispute

  1. The dispute arises
  2. The parties try to negotiate
  3. A letter of demand is sent
  4. The parties attend mediation
  5. The plaintiff files a statement of claim
  6. The court hears the case
  7. The court gives judgment and orders a remedy

items.name: Spot the mistake
items.html:
This paragraph answers: "Outline the difference between criminal and civil cases."

In a criminal case the plaintiff prosecution must prove the offence on the balance of probabilities beyond reasonable doubt. If the accused is found guilty, the court imposes a remedy sanction. In a civil case the person who sues is called the accused plaintiff, and a successful claim usually ends in an award of damages.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Why does the law give young people special protection?

  1. Young people have more money than adults
  2. Young people are still developing and are more vulnerable to harm and exploitation
  3. Young people cannot break the law
  4. The Constitution requires it

Why B: The law recognises limited maturity and experience, while giving more independence as capacity grows.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is the minimum age of criminal responsibility in NSW?

  1. 8
  2. 10
  3. 14
  4. 16

Why B: A child under 10 cannot be charged. From 10 to under 14, doli incapax applies.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What does a high rate of recidivism among young people who have been in detention suggest?

  1. Detention is working well as a deterrent
  2. Detention often fails to address the causes of offending
  3. Young people commit more serious crimes than adults
  4. The age of criminal responsibility is too high

Why B: If many young people reoffend after detention, rehabilitation has not been achieved. This supports diversion.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which international treaty sets out the rights of people under 18?

  1. Refugee Convention
  2. Convention on the Rights of the Child
  3. Rome Statute
  4. International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights

Why B: Australia ratified the Convention in 1990. It says the best interests of the child must be a primary consideration.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which NSW court hears most criminal matters involving people under 18?

  1. The Local Court
  2. The Children's Court
  3. The District Court
  4. The Coroner's Court

Why B: The Children's Court is a closed, specialist court. Very serious offences can be sent to a higher court.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which Act sets up warnings, cautions and youth justice conferences in NSW?

  1. Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW)
  2. Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW)
  3. Bail Act 2013 (NSW)
  4. Crimes Act 1900 (NSW)

Why B: The Act diverts young people who admit less serious offences away from court.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which body advocates for the rights of children and young people across Australia?

  1. The National Children's Commissioner
  2. The Director of Public Prosecutions
  3. The Reserve Bank of Australia
  4. The State Parole Authority

Why A: The Commissioner sits within the Australian Human Rights Commission. NSW also has an Advocate for Children and Young People.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which is a barrier to justice for many young people?

  1. They are not allowed to have a lawyer
  2. They often do not know their rights or how to get legal help
  3. They cannot be witnesses
  4. Courts are open only on weekends

Why B: Lack of knowledge, cost, distance and distrust of authority all limit access. Legal Aid NSW runs a Youth Hotline to help.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is the difference between an asylum seeker and a refugee?

  1. An asylum seeker has been found to be owed protection; a refugee has not
  2. An asylum seeker's claim for protection has not yet been decided; a refugee meets the legal definition
  3. They are the same thing
  4. A refugee always arrives by boat

Why B: Every refugee was first an asylum seeker. How a person arrives does not decide whether they are a refugee.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which treaty defines who is a refugee and sets out the duty of non-refoulement?

  1. Convention on the Rights of the Child
  2. Convention relating to the Status of Refugees (1951)
  3. Universal Declaration of Human Rights
  4. Rome Statute

Why B: The Convention and its 1967 Protocol bind Australia in international law.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which Act governs visas, detention and the removal of non-citizens in Australia?

  1. Migration Act 1958 (Cth)
  2. Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth)
  3. Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth)
  4. Crimes Act 1914 (Cth)

Why A: The Act requires the detention of unlawful non-citizens and sets the tests for protection visas.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What did the High Court decide in NZYQ v Minister for Immigration (2023)?

  1. That offshore processing is unlawful
  2. That indefinite immigration detention is unlawful where there is no real prospect of removing the person in the reasonably foreseeable future
  3. That all asylum seekers must be given permanent visas
  4. That the Refugee Convention is part of the Constitution

Why B: The decision overturned Al-Kateb v Godwin (2004) and led to the release of people held in long-term detention.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which body can review many decisions to refuse a protection visa?

  1. The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal
  2. The Administrative Review Tribunal
  3. The Children's Court
  4. The International Criminal Court

Why B: The Tribunal replaced the Administrative Appeals Tribunal in October 2024 and conducts merits review of Commonwealth decisions.

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain what is meant by the "evolving capacity" of young people, using TWO examples of age limits in the law.

  • Defines evolving capacity (1)
  • The law gives rights and responsibilities in stages (1)
  • Two accurate examples, such as criminal responsibility at 10, a learner licence at 16 or voting at 18 (2)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain how the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) aims to achieve justice for young people.

  • It provides warnings, cautions and youth justice conferences (1)
  • Court is kept for more serious matters (1)
  • Young people avoid a criminal record for minor offending (1)
  • Conferences let victims take part and repair harm (1)
  • A limit, such as uneven use across groups (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Assess the responsiveness of the legal system to asylum seekers and refugees.

  • An indicator of success, such as merits review or access to the courts (1)
  • A case or law that shows it, such as NZYQ (2023) (1)
  • A barrier, such as mandatory detention or offshore processing (1)
  • A second barrier, such as delay, language or limited legal aid (1)
  • The role of advocates, such as the Australian Human Rights Commission or non-government organisations (1)
  • A judgement (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
Kai, aged 15, is stopped by police at a train station after a security guard says he saw Kai take a pair of headphones from a shop. Kai admits he took them. It is his first contact with police. The officer wants to take a formal statement from him straight away, on the platform.

(a) Outline TWO rights Kai has when police question him. (2 marks)

  • The right to silence, apart from giving his name and address (1)
  • The right to have a responsible adult present and to get legal advice, for example from the Legal Aid Youth Hotline (1)

(b) Explain the most likely outcome for Kai and why. (3 marks)

  • A caution, or possibly a warning, under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) (1)
  • The offence is minor, he admits it and it is his first (1)
  • Diversion aims to keep young people out of court (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
Samira fled her country after she was threatened because of her work as a journalist. She arrived in Australia on a student visa and has now applied for a protection visa. A departmental officer refuses her application, saying she could safely live in another part of her country.

(a) Explain whether Samira is an asylum seeker or a refugee at this point. (2 marks)

  • She is an asylum seeker because her claim has not been finally decided (1)
  • She would be a refugee if she is found to have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention reason, such as political opinion (1)

(b) Outline what Samira can do about the refusal. (3 marks)

  • Apply for merits review by the Administrative Review Tribunal (1)
  • Seek help from a refugee legal service or advocacy group (1)
  • Judicial review by a court is possible if there was a legal error (1)

items.html:
Sort each item under the correct heading.

ItemCategory
