Decisions can be reviewed by an independent tribunalIndicator of success in achieving justice
Diversion keeps most young people out of courtIndicator of success in achieving justice

items.name: Spot the mistake
items.html:
This paragraph answers: "Outline how the law treats a 12-year-old accused of an offence in NSW."

In NSW a child under 12 10 cannot be charged with an offence. A 12-year-old is covered by doli incapax, which means the defence prosecution must prove the child knew the act was seriously wrong. The matter would be heard in the Local Court Children's Court, which is open closed to the public.

items.name: Extended response
items.html:
Explain how laws are made in Australia. In your answer, refer to both parliament and the courts.

  • Statute law: the stages of a bill and royal assent
  • Common law: precedent, ratio decidendi and the court hierarchy
  • The relationship between the two: statute overrides common law; courts interpret statutes
  • The Constitution sets the limits of law-making power
  • At least one named Act and one named case

Plan

  • How parliament makes law
  • How courts make law
  • How the two work together
  • Conclusion

items.name: Extended response
items.html:
Compare how criminal law and civil law resolve disputes.

  • Purpose, parties, burden and standard of proof
  • Process: prosecution and trial against claim, negotiation and hearing
  • Outcomes: sanctions against remedies
  • A named example or case for each
  • Similarities as well as differences

Plan

  • Purpose and parties
  • Proof
  • Outcomes
  • Conclusion: two systems for two kinds of wrong

items.name: Extended response
items.html:
Assess the outcomes of law reform in relation to native title.

  • Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992) and the rejection of terra nullius
  • Native Title Act 1993 (Cth) and later amendments
  • Benefits: recognition, successful claims, agreements over land use
  • Limitations: the burden of proving continuous connection, extinguishment, delay and cost
  • A judgement

Plan

  • What changed
  • Benefits
  • Limitations
  • Judgement

items.name: Extended response
items.html:
To what extent does the legal system achieve justice for young people?

  • Protection in domestic and international law
  • Police powers and safeguards for young people
  • The Children's Court and diversion under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW)
  • Barriers: knowledge, access to legal help, over-representation of some groups, detention
  • A judgement on extent, with evidence

Plan

  • Protections that work
  • Diversion
  • Barriers
  • Judgement

items.name: Extended response
items.html:
Assess the responsiveness of the legal system to asylum seekers and refugees.

  • International obligations: the Refugee Convention and non-refoulement
  • Migration Act 1958 (Cth): detention and visas
  • Review by the Administrative Review Tribunal and the courts, including NZYQ (2023)
  • Advocates: the Australian Human Rights Commission and non-government organisations
  • Barriers: delay, detention, limited legal help
  • A judgement

Plan

  • Obligations
  • Domestic law and review
  • Barriers
  • Judgement

items.name: TEEACL paragraph
items.html:
Explain why the rule of law is important in Australia.

  • A clear statement of what the rule of law means
  • Evidence: an example such as courts reviewing government decisions
  • Explanation of how it limits power
  • Counterpoint: unequal access to legal help weakens equality before the law
  • A link back to the question

items.name: TEEACL paragraph
items.html:
Assess the effectiveness of tribunals in resolving disputes between individuals and the state.

  • A judgement
  • Evidence: a named tribunal and what it can do
  • Analysis against accessibility or resource efficiency
  • Counterpoint: delay, or limits on what can be reviewed
  • A link back to the question

items.name: TEEACL paragraph
items.html:
Assess the effectiveness of the social media minimum age law as a response to changing technology.

  • A judgement
  • Evidence: Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act 2024 (Cth) and who must comply
  • Analysis against enforceability or responsiveness
  • Counterpoint: age checks can be avoided, and there are privacy concerns
  • A link back to the question

items.name: TEEACL paragraph
items.html:
Assess the effectiveness of diversion in achieving justice for young people.

  • A judgement
  • Evidence: Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) and a finding from a named source
  • Analysis against the capacity to meet society's needs
  • Counterpoint: diversion is not used equally for all groups
  • A link back to the question

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is the main difference between a law and a rule?

  1. Laws are written down; rules are not
  2. Laws apply to everyone in society and are enforced by the state
  3. Rules carry heavier penalties than laws
  4. Laws are made by schools and clubs

Why B: Rules apply to members of a group, such as a school. Laws bind the whole community and are enforced by police and courts.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which of the following is a characteristic of an effective law?

  1. It is kept secret until it is enforced
  2. It is known, clear and able to be enforced
  3. It applies only to some people
  4. It never changes

Why B: People can only obey laws they can find out about and understand, and a law that cannot be enforced will be ignored.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
A person sues a builder for failing to finish a house. Which area of law is this?

  1. Criminal law
  2. Constitutional law
  3. Private (civil) law
  4. International law

Why C: A dispute between individuals over a contract is private law. The state is not a party.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
How is Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Customary Lore traditionally passed on?

  1. Through Acts of parliament
  2. Orally, through stories, song, dance and ceremony
  3. Through written court judgments
  4. Through international treaties

Why B: Customary Lore is an oral tradition. Elders hold the knowledge and pass it on to the next generation.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which statement about Customary Lore is most accurate?

  1. It is the same for all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples
  2. It differs between nations and language groups but shares common features, such as connection to Country
  3. It deals only with criminal matters
  4. It was created by the British in 1788

Why B: There are many nations, each with its own Lore. Shared features include kinship, Country and the role of Elders.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which part of a judgment creates a binding precedent?

  1. The obiter dicta
  2. The ratio decidendi
  3. The dissenting judgment
  4. The orders for costs

Why B: The ratio decidendi is the legal reasoning needed for the decision. Lower courts in the same hierarchy must follow it.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
A District Court judge in NSW is deciding a case. Which decision is binding on that judge?

  1. A decision of the Local Court
  2. A decision of the Supreme Court of Victoria
  3. A decision of the High Court of Australia
  4. A decision of a court in England

Why C: Decisions of higher courts in the same hierarchy bind lower courts. Decisions from other hierarchies are persuasive only.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is the final step before a bill becomes an Act?

  1. The first reading
  2. The second reading debate
  3. Royal assent
  4. The committee stage

Why C: After both houses pass the bill, the Governor-General (or a state Governor) gives royal assent.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which is the highest court in Australia?

  1. The Supreme Court of NSW
  2. The Federal Court of Australia
  3. The High Court of Australia
  4. The District Court of NSW

Why C: The High Court is the final court of appeal and decides cases about the Constitution.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is the role of the Coroner's Court?

  1. To sentence people convicted of murder
  2. To inquire into the cause and manner of unexplained deaths, and into fires and explosions
  3. To hear appeals from the Local Court
  4. To settle family disputes

Why B: A coroner holds an inquest to make findings and recommendations. A coroner does not decide guilt.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What happens under s 109 of the Constitution when a valid Commonwealth law and a state law are inconsistent?

  1. The state law prevails
  2. The Commonwealth law prevails and the state law is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency
  3. Both laws are invalid
  4. The High Court holds a referendum

Why B: Section 109 settles clashes in areas of concurrent power in favour of the Commonwealth.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is needed for a referendum to change the Constitution to succeed?

  1. A majority in the House of Representatives only
  2. A majority of voters nationally and a majority of voters in a majority of states
  3. The agreement of all six state premiers
  4. A unanimous decision of the High Court

Why B: Section 128 requires this double majority. Only 8 of 45 proposals have passed.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which arm of government interprets and applies the law?

  1. The legislature
  2. The executive
  3. The judiciary
  4. The public service

Why C: The legislature makes law, the executive carries it out and the judiciary (the courts) interprets it.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is a treaty?

  1. A law passed by the United Nations that binds every country
  2. A written agreement between states that binds the states that ratify it
  3. A decision of the International Court of Justice
  4. A custom followed within one country

Why B: Treaties bind only the states that agree to them. In Australia a treaty also needs legislation before it applies in domestic law.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which of the following is a source of rights in Australia?

  1. A national bill of rights
  2. The Constitution, statute law, common law and international law
  3. The decisions of juries
  4. The rules of political parties

Why B: Australia has no national bill of rights. Rights come from several sources, each with limits.

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain how the doctrine of precedent promotes fairness and consistency.

  • Courts follow earlier decisions of higher courts in the same hierarchy (1)
  • Like cases are decided alike (1)
  • People and lawyers can predict how the law will apply (1)
  • Judges can still distinguish a case on its facts, which allows the law to develop (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain why the separation of powers is important.

  • Names the three arms and what each does (1)
  • No single body makes, carries out and judges the law (1)
  • Independent courts can check the other arms (1)
  • This protects individuals from the abuse of power (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Describe the role of Elders in maintaining Customary Lore.

  • Elders hold knowledge of Lore and pass it on (1)
  • They teach through story, ceremony and example (1)
  • They help resolve disputes through discussion and mediation (1)
  • They are involved in programs such as circle sentencing (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain how state sovereignty affects the enforcement of international law.

  • Defines state sovereignty (1)
  • States choose whether to sign and ratify treaties (1)
  • There is no world police force; enforcement relies on cooperation and pressure (1)
  • An example of a state not complying (1)
  • Sovereignty also lets states pass laws to give effect to their obligations (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
The NSW Parliament passes a law that says shops may refuse to accept cash. A year later the Commonwealth Parliament passes a valid law, under its currency power, that says all shops must accept cash for purchases under $500. A shop owner in Sydney does not know which law to follow.

(a) Identify the section of the Constitution that resolves this conflict. (1 marks)

Section 109.

(b) Explain which law the shop owner must follow and why. (3 marks)

  • The Commonwealth law (1)
  • Where a valid Commonwealth law and a state law are inconsistent, the Commonwealth law prevails (1)
  • The state law is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency (1)

items.name: Put in order
items.html:
How a bill becomes an Act of the Commonwealth Parliament

  1. The bill is drafted
  2. First reading: the bill is introduced
  3. Second reading: the minister explains the bill and it is debated
  4. Consideration in detail: the bill is examined clause by clause
  5. Third reading: the house votes on the bill
  6. The bill goes through the same stages in the other house
  7. The Governor-General gives royal assent

Courts that hear criminal matters in NSW, from lowest to highest

  4. Court of Criminal Appeal
  5. High Court of Australia

items.name: Spot the mistake
items.html:
This paragraph answers: "Outline how the Australian Constitution can be changed."

The Constitution came into effect on 1 January 1900 1901. It can be changed only by a referendum under section 109 128. A proposal must first be passed by the High Court Parliament. It then needs a majority of voters across Australia and a majority of voters in at least three four of the six states. This is called a simple double majority.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which is an example of the changing nature of crime?

  1. The growth of online fraud, scams and identity theft
  2. The abolition of all summary offences
  3. The end of police discretion
  4. The removal of juries from every trial

Why A: Technology has created new offences and new ways to commit old ones, and the law has had to respond.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
How does police discretion support the rule of law when it is used properly?

  1. It lets police ignore legislation
  2. It lets police respond in proportion to the offence, within limits set by law and guidelines
  3. It replaces the role of the courts
  4. It applies only to indictable offences

Why B: Warnings, cautions and fines save court time for serious matters. The risk is inconsistent or biased use.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Why can a long period on remand be seen as conflicting with the presumption of innocence?

  1. Remand is a sentence imposed after conviction
  2. A person on remand is held in custody although they have not been found guilty
  3. Remand applies only to people who plead guilty
  4. People on remand cannot have a lawyer

Why B: Time on remand can cost a person their job or housing, and some are later acquitted or given a non-custodial sentence.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which is an example of a pre-trial process?

  1. Sentencing
  2. Parole
  3. Committal proceedings and charge negotiation
  4. An appeal to the High Court

Why C: Pre-trial steps decide whether and how a matter goes to trial, and encourage early guilty pleas.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which is an argument for a judge-alone trial rather than a jury trial?

  1. A judge gives written reasons, and the trial avoids jurors being swayed by pre-trial publicity
  2. A judge represents a cross-section of the community
  3. Judge-alone trials always take longer
  4. The accused cannot appeal a jury verdict

Why A: Reasons make the decision open to review. The main argument for juries is community participation.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which organisation provides legal services designed for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in NSW?

  1. The Aboriginal Legal Service
  2. The State Parole Authority
  3. The Sentencing Council
  4. The Judicial Commission

Why A: The Service gives culturally appropriate advice and representation, including through the custody notification service.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which is a diversionary program available to some adult offenders in NSW?

  1. The Drug Court program
  2. A standard non-parole period
  3. A continuing detention order
  4. A committal hearing

Why A: The Drug Court supervises treatment for drug-dependent offenders as an alternative to prison.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which sentencing options are designed to be culturally appropriate for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander offenders?

  1. Circle sentencing and the Youth Koori Court
  2. Mandatory sentencing and standard non-parole periods
  3. Fines and forfeiture
  4. Extradition and deportation

Why A: Elders and respected community members take part, which aims to make the process meaningful and to reduce reoffending.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Who decides how a prisoner in NSW is classified and where they are placed?

  1. The sentencing judge
  2. Corrective Services NSW
  3. The jury
  4. The Director of Public Prosecutions

Why B: Classification reflects risk and affects access to programs and work, and so to rehabilitation.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is the main criticism of continuing detention orders for high-risk offenders?

  1. They are made by police without any court hearing
  2. They keep a person in custody after their sentence has ended, on the basis of what they might do
  3. They apply to every offender
  4. They cannot be reviewed

Why B: The orders protect the community but sit uneasily with the principle that a person is punished only for what they have done.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Why do nation-states need international relations?

  1. Because problems such as conflict, trade, climate and migration cross borders and cannot be solved by one state alone
  2. Because the United Nations makes laws for every state
  3. Because state sovereignty no longer exists
  4. Because every state has the same legal system

Why A: Cooperation through treaties and organisations lets states manage shared problems while keeping their sovereignty.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which is an example of a regional intergovernmental organisation?

  1. Amnesty International
  2. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)
  3. The International Committee of the Red Cross
  4. Human Rights Watch

Why B: Its members are states. Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch are non-government organisations.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which statement about the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples is correct?

  1. It is a binding treaty enforced by the International Criminal Court
  2. It is a non-binding declaration that sets standards, including the right to self-determination
  3. It applies only in Australia
  4. It replaced the Universal Declaration of Human Rights

Why B: The General Assembly adopted it in 2007. Australia voted against it then and endorsed it in 2009.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
How does the Universal Periodic Review monitor human rights?

  1. Judges try the leaders of each state
  2. The human rights record of every United Nations member state is reviewed by other states through the Human Rights Council
  3. Non-government organisations vote on sanctions
  4. The Security Council inspects each state every year

Why B: The review produces recommendations. States are not forced to accept them.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What does the Human Rights (Parliamentary Scrutiny) Act 2011 (Cth) require?

  1. Courts must strike down laws that breach human rights
  2. Each new bill must come with a statement of compatibility with human rights, and a parliamentary committee examines bills
  3. A referendum on a bill of rights
  4. Treaties to apply automatically

Why B: The Act builds rights into law-making, but parliament can still pass a law that is not compatible.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which is a limit on the role of the media in promoting human rights?

  1. The media cannot report on other countries
  2. Coverage can be selective, short-lived or shaped by commercial and political interests
  3. The media is controlled by the United Nations
  4. Journalists are not allowed to interview victims

Why B: Media attention can force action, but issues that are not covered may be ignored.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
How does Australian law respond to forced marriage?

  1. It is a criminal offence under Commonwealth law
  2. It is lawful with parental consent
  3. It is dealt with only by the Children's Court
  4. It is not recognised as a legal issue

Why A: Forced marriage offences were added to the Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth) in 2013. Under-reporting makes cases hard to identify.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What is the aim of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Child Placement Principle?

  1. To place every child in residential care
  2. To keep children who cannot live at home connected to family, community, culture and Country
  3. To speed up adoption
  4. To move child protection cases to the High Court

Why B: The Principle responds to the harm done by past removal policies and is part of NSW child protection law.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
What makes a financial agreement between partners binding under the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth)?

  1. It is agreed verbally
  2. It is in writing, signed, and each person has had independent legal advice
  3. It is approved by the Children's Court
  4. It is made after a divorce only

Why B: Without independent advice for each person, a court can set the agreement aside.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
How does native title differ from Torrens title?

  1. Native title is a registered freehold interest that can be sold
  2. Native title recognises rights under traditional laws and customs and cannot be sold like freehold
  3. Torrens title applies only to Crown land
  4. There is no difference

Why B: Native title is a communal set of rights that depends on continuing connection. Torrens title is ownership recorded on the state register.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Why is culturally appropriate housing important for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples?

  1. It costs less to build
  2. Housing designed and managed with communities supports kinship obligations, connection to Country and better health
  3. It is required by the Constitution
  4. It replaces the need for land rights

Why B: Standard housing and rules can clash with family obligations, and overcrowding harms health and education.

items.name: Multiple choice
items.html:
Which is a barrier to justice in property disputes?

  1. The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal charges no fees at all
  2. Complex rules, legal costs and language barriers discourage people from enforcing their rights
  3. Tenants are banned from applying to the Tribunal
  4. Mediation is illegal in NSW

Why B: Rights that people cannot use in practice give little protection. Advice services and interpreters reduce the barrier.

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain the impact of remand on the accused and on society.

  • Defines remand (1)
  • Impact on the accused: loss of liberty, work, housing or family contact before any finding of guilt (1)
  • It is harder to prepare a defence from custody (1)
  • Impact on society: protection from risk, but a high cost and crowded prisons (1)
  • A link to the presumption of innocence (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Outline TWO reasons for and TWO reasons against the use of juries in criminal trials.

  • For: community participation; the decision is shared among twelve people (2)
  • Against: no reasons are given; jurors may be influenced by the media or struggle with complex evidence (2)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain the purpose of parole and the conditions that may apply.

  • Supervised release for the last part of a sentence (1)
  • It supports reintegration and reduces reoffending (1)
  • Conditions such as reporting, where to live and attending programs (1)
  • Parole can be revoked if conditions are breached (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain the impact of state sovereignty on the changing global community.

  • Defines state sovereignty (1)
  • States remain the main actors and must consent to be bound (1)
  • Global problems and organisations put pressure on sovereignty (1)
  • An example, such as a state refusing to follow a decision of an international body (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Discuss the debate over the need for a human rights framework in Australia.

  • Current protection is spread across the Constitution, statute and common law (1)
  • For: clearer rights, protection of minorities, education (1 to 2)
  • Against: parliamentary sovereignty, power shifted to judges, cost (1 to 2)
  • Refers to an existing model, such as the Victorian Charter or the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld) (1)
  • Presents both sides (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain the challenges in identifying and responding to forced marriage in Australia.

  • Defines forced marriage and notes it is a crime (1)
  • Victims are often young and under family pressure, so they may not report (1)
  • Marriages may take place overseas (1)
  • Responses include support services, protection orders and education (1)

items.name: Short answer
items.html:
Explain the impact of homelessness on the enjoyment of human rights.

  • Names the right to adequate housing (1)
  • Health: harder to stay well or get treatment (1)
  • Education and work: hard to attend without a stable address (1)
  • Safety and privacy are at risk (1)
  • Rights are connected: losing one affects the others (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
Dev, aged 28, is charged with a serious assault. He has no criminal record, a full-time job and lives with his parents. The alleged victim is a neighbour. The case has been in the news for a week, with headlines calling Dev a "thug". His trial in the District Court is nine months away.

(a) Explain what a court would consider in deciding whether to grant Dev bail. (3 marks)

  • Whether there is an unacceptable risk, such as endangering the victim or interfering with witnesses (1)
  • His community ties, job and lack of record reduce the risk of failing to appear (1)
  • Conditions, such as no contact with the neighbour, could manage the risk (1)

(b) Explain why Dev might apply for a judge-alone trial. (3 marks)

  • Pre-trial publicity may prejudice jurors (1)
  • A judge gives reasons, which can be tested on appeal (1)
  • The court decides whether a judge-alone trial is in the interests of justice (1)

items.name: Scenario
items.html:
Thanh arrived in Australia two years ago and speaks limited English. He rents a unit with his family. Mould has spread through the bedroom and his daughter's asthma is worse. The agent has ignored his messages for a month. Thanh is afraid that if he complains, the family will lose their home.

(a) Identify the landlord's obligation and the body that can enforce it. (2 marks)

  • To provide and maintain premises that are fit to live in and in reasonable repair (1)
  • The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (1)

(b) Explain the barriers Thanh faces in accessing justice and how they could be reduced. (4 marks)

  • Language: forms and hearings are in English (1)
  • Fear of losing the tenancy, and not knowing the law (1)
  • Interpreters are available at the Tribunal, and tenant advice services give free help (1)
  • The law limits retaliatory evictions and now requires a reason to end a tenancy (1)

items.name: Extended response
items.html:
To what extent do sentencing and post-sentencing measures balance the rights of victims, offenders and society?

  • The purposes of sentencing and how they compete
  • Judicial discretion, guidelines, and aggravating and mitigating factors
  • Victim impact statements
  • Custodial and non-custodial penalties, with evidence on reoffending
  • Diversionary and culturally appropriate options
  • Parole, and detention and supervision orders for high-risk offenders
  • A sustained judgement

Plan

  • Sentencing: weighing purposes
  • Victims: a voice but not a veto
  • Offenders: rehabilitation and diversion
  • Society: protection after the sentence ends
  • Judgement

items.name: Extended response
items.html:
Evaluate the effectiveness of legal and non-legal measures in protecting ONE human right.

  • Names the right and where it is recognised
  • International protection: instruments, monitoring and courts, and their limits
  • Australian protection: the Constitution, statute, common law, the Australian Human Rights Commission, courts and tribunals
  • Promotion by non-government organisations and the media
  • A judgement using criteria such as enforceability and the protection of individual rights

Plan

  • International protection and state sovereignty
  • Domestic protection without a national framework
  • Non-legal promotion
  • Judgement

items.name: TEEACL paragraph
items.html:
Assess the impact of diversionary programs in reducing recidivism.

  • A judgement
  • Evidence: a named program, such as the Drug Court or circle sentencing, and a finding from a named source
  • Analysis against resource efficiency or the capacity to meet society's needs
  • Counterpoint: limited places and strict eligibility
  • A link back to the question

items.name: TEEACL paragraph
items.html:
Evaluate the effectiveness of government measures to address housing affordability.

  • A judgement
  • Evidence: a named measure and a statistic from a named source
  • Analysis against the capacity to meet society's needs
  • Counterpoint: measures that add to demand can push prices higher
  • A link back to the question

items.name: Sort and classify
items.html:
Sort each measure under the stage of the criminal justice system where it is used.

ItemCategory
Victim impact statementSentencing
Intensive correction orderSentencing
Aggravating and mitigating factorsSentencing
Circle sentencingSentencing
Security classificationPost-sentencing
ParolePost-sentencing
Extended supervision orderPost-sentencing
Continuing detention orderPost-sentencing

items.name: Compare table
items.html:
Complete the table to compare a jury trial with a judge-alone trial.

Jury trialJudge-alone trial
Who decides the verdictTwelve members of the community(given) A judge
Reasons for the verdictNone are givenWritten reasons are given
Main strength(given) Community participation and shared responsibilityLegal expertise and less risk of prejudice from publicity
Main weaknessJurors may not follow complex evidence or directionsOne person decides, without community input

items.name: Spot the mistake
items.html:
This paragraph answers: "Outline how high-risk offenders can be managed after their sentence ends in NSW."

Under the Crimes (High Risk Offenders) Act 2006 (NSW), the Local Court Supreme Court can make orders about serious sex or violence offenders who still pose an unacceptable risk. An intensive correction extended supervision order lets the person live in the community under strict conditions. A continuing parole detention order keeps the person in custody. These orders are made before the trial near the end of the sentence.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A crime is an act or omission against the community that is punishable by the state.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Actus reus is the mental element of a crime.

Corrected: Actus reus is the physical element of a crime.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Recklessness can satisfy the mental element of an offence.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Indictable offences are finalised by a magistrate sitting alone.

Corrected: Indictable offences are usually tried by a judge and jury in a higher court.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Motive is an element the prosecution must always prove.

Corrected: The prosecution must prove actus reus and mens rea, not motive.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Criminal negligence can amount to mens rea for some offences, such as manslaughter.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Police can arrest without a warrant if they suspect on reasonable grounds that a person has committed an offence and the arrest is reasonably necessary.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Bail means the accused has been found not guilty.

Corrected: Bail is the conditional release of an accused person until the case is heard.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: An accused who is refused bail is held on remand.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Police need a warrant for every search.

Corrected: Police can search without a warrant in some situations, such as on reasonable suspicion.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A court attendance notice tells an accused when and where to appear in court.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A person on remand has been convicted.

Corrected: A person on remand has not been convicted and is presumed innocent.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The burden of proof in a criminal trial rests on the prosecution.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The Director of Public Prosecutions represents the accused.

Corrected: The Director of Public Prosecutions prosecutes serious offences on behalf of the state.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Public Defenders are barristers who represent people who have been granted legal aid in serious matters.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A magistrate sits with a jury in the Local Court.

Corrected: A magistrate sits alone, without a jury.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The Court of Criminal Appeal hears appeals against conviction and sentence from the District and Supreme Courts.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The accused must give evidence at their trial.

Corrected: The accused cannot be forced to give evidence.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Imprisonment is a sentence of last resort in NSW.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A guideline judgment is a law passed by parliament.

Corrected: A guideline judgment is issued by the Court of Criminal Appeal to guide sentencing for an offence.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The prosecution can appeal against a sentence it considers manifestly inadequate.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A fine is a custodial sentence.

Corrected: A fine is a non-custodial penalty.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A standard non-parole period guides the court when it sentences for certain serious offences.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The maximum penalty must be given for every offence.

Corrected: The maximum penalty is reserved for the worst cases.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A child under 10 cannot be charged with a criminal offence in NSW.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The Children's Court is open to the public.

Corrected: The Children's Court is a closed court.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Detention is a last resort for young offenders.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A young offender is sentenced under the same Act as an adult.

Corrected: Penalties for children are set out in the Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW).

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The Convention on the Rights of the Child says the best interests of the child must be a primary consideration.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The International Criminal Court was set up by the Rome Statute.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The International Criminal Court tries countries rather than people.

Corrected: The International Criminal Court tries individuals.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Extradition is the surrender of a person by one state to another to face trial or punishment.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Transnational crimes can only be prosecuted by international courts.

Corrected: Transnational crimes are prosecuted under the domestic law of the states involved.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: State sovereignty can limit the enforcement of international criminal law.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A marriage is void if one person was already legally married to someone else.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A couple must be married for the law to recognise their relationship.

Corrected: De facto relationships are also recognised by the law.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Both parents have parental responsibility for a child unless a court orders otherwise.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Children have no say in parenting disputes.

Corrected: A court considers the child's views, giving them weight according to the child's age and maturity.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A marriage celebrant must be authorised under the Marriage Act 1961 (Cth).

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Australia has had no-fault divorce since the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) began.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A couple married for less than two years cannot divorce.

Corrected: They can, but they must usually attend counselling first or get the court's permission.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Non-financial contributions, such as caring for children, count in a property settlement.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Only the victim can apply for an apprehended domestic violence order.

Corrected: Police can and often must apply on the victim's behalf.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Breaching an apprehended domestic violence order is a criminal offence.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A parenting plan is enforceable in the same way as a court order.

Corrected: A parenting plan is not legally enforceable; a parenting order is.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Same-sex couples have been able to marry in Australia since December 2017.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Commercial surrogacy is legal in NSW.

Corrected: Commercial surrogacy is a criminal offence in NSW; only altruistic surrogacy is allowed.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Teachers in NSW are mandatory reporters of children at risk of significant harm.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The Family Court decides whether a child is removed from an unsafe home.

Corrected: The Children's Court of NSW makes care and protection orders.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Same-sex couples can adopt children in NSW.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Human rights are described as inherent because people have them from birth.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is a binding treaty.

Corrected: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is a declaration and is not legally binding.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights were both adopted in 1966.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Peace rights are individual rights.

Corrected: Peace rights are collective rights.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The movement to abolish slavery was one of the first international human rights campaigns.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Universal suffrage means only property owners can vote.

Corrected: Universal suffrage means all adult citizens can vote.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The five permanent members of the Security Council each hold a veto.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Individuals can bring a case to the International Court of Justice.

Corrected: Only states can be parties to cases before the International Court of Justice.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Non-government organisations can "name and shame" governments by publishing reports.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: United Nations General Assembly resolutions are binding on all states.

Corrected: General Assembly resolutions are recommendations and are not binding.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: State sovereignty means a state has authority over its own territory and people.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Australia has no national Charter of Rights.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The Constitution expressly protects freedom of speech.

Corrected: The High Court has found an implied freedom of political communication; there is no express right to free speech.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Victoria, the Australian Capital Territory and Queensland each have a human rights Act.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The Australian Human Rights Commission can make binding court orders.

Corrected: The Commission conciliates complaints; binding orders are made by courts.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth) gives effect to an international convention.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The right to adequate housing is recognised in the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The Australian Constitution guarantees a right to housing.

Corrected: There is no constitutional right to housing in Australia.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A deposit of about 10 per cent is usually paid when contracts are exchanged.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A cooling-off period applies to homes bought at auction.

Corrected: No cooling-off period applies at auction.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Under Torrens title, the register is conclusive evidence of ownership.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A mortgage transfers ownership of the home to the bank.

Corrected: The borrower owns the home; the bank holds security over it.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A landlord in NSW must usually give notice before entering a rented property.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A landlord can keep the bond in a personal bank account.

Corrected: The bond must be lodged with NSW Fair Trading.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A tenant can ask the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal to order repairs.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Boarders and lodgers have exactly the same rights as tenants.

Corrected: Boarders and lodgers are covered by different and weaker rules.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A tenant is not responsible for fair wear and tear.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: It is unlawful in NSW to refuse to rent a home to someone because of their race.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Homelessness only means sleeping on the street.

Corrected: Homelessness also includes couch surfing, crisis accommodation and severe overcrowding.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Family and domestic violence is a leading cause of homelessness for women and children.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Social housing is provided only by the government.

Corrected: Community housing providers and Aboriginal housing organisations also provide social housing.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Commonwealth Rent Assistance is a payment that helps eligible people with private rent.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Changing social values are a reason for law reform.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A law reform commission can pass laws.

Corrected: A law reform commission can only recommend changes; parliament passes laws.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A royal commission can compel witnesses to give evidence.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Courts can reform any area of law whenever they choose.

Corrected: Courts can change the law only through the cases brought before them.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Parliament can pass a statute to override a court's decision on the common law.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Law reform always achieves its aims.

Corrected: Reform can have limits, such as weak enforcement or unintended effects.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The Mabo decision overturned the doctrine of terra nullius.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Native title was created by an Act of the NSW Parliament.

Corrected: Native title was recognised by the High Court at common law and then regulated by the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth).

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Under the Aboriginal Land Rights Act 1983 (NSW), land councils can claim certain Crown land.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Under the social media minimum age law, children who open an account commit an offence.

Corrected: The duty and the penalties fall on the platforms, not on children or parents.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The social media minimum age in Australia is 16.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The standard of proof is higher in a criminal case than in a civil case.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The victim decides whether to prosecute a serious crime.

Corrected: The state decides whether to prosecute.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A single act, such as an assault, can lead to both a criminal case and a civil case.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A person found liable in a civil case is sent to prison.

Corrected: A person found liable is usually ordered to pay damages.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A contract can be binding even if it is not in writing.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: In negligence, the plaintiff must prove the defendant intended to cause harm.

Corrected: The plaintiff must prove a duty of care, a breach and damage; intention is not required.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Administrative law lets people challenge decisions made by government bodies.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: An ombudsman can send a public servant to prison.

Corrected: An ombudsman investigates complaints and makes recommendations.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The media and non-government organisations can help people in disputes with the state by drawing attention to their cases.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Judicial review lets a court replace a government decision with the one it prefers.

Corrected: Judicial review only decides whether the decision was lawfully made.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Tribunals are generally cheaper and less formal than courts.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A child under 10 cannot be held criminally responsible in NSW.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The Children's Court is open to the public and the media can name the child.

Corrected: The Children's Court is closed and children generally cannot be named.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Australia has ratified the Convention on the Rights of the Child.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Police can never arrest a person under 18.

Corrected: Police can arrest a young person, but arrest and detention should be a last resort.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A youth justice conference can include the victim.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Recidivism means a young person has been diverted from court.

Corrected: Recidivism means reoffending.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: It is lawful under international law to seek asylum.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A person who arrives without a visa cannot be a refugee.

Corrected: Refugee status depends on a well-founded fear of persecution, not on how a person arrives.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Non-refoulement means a refugee must not be returned to a place where they face persecution.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The Refugee Convention is automatically part of Australian law.

Corrected: Treaties apply in Australia only as far as parliament has enacted them, mainly through the Migration Act 1958 (Cth).

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The Australian Human Rights Commission can inquire into the treatment of people in immigration detention.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Laws apply to everyone in society, while rules apply only to members of a particular group.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Obiter dicta are binding on lower courts.

Corrected: Obiter dicta are persuasive only; the ratio decidendi is binding.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Statute law overrides common law where the two conflict.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A bill becomes law as soon as the lower house passes it.

Corrected: A bill must pass both houses and receive royal assent.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Delegated legislation is made by bodies such as local councils under a power given by parliament.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Criminal law is a type of private law.

Corrected: Criminal law is a type of public law.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The High Court of Australia can hear appeals from state Supreme Courts.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The Local Court hears murder trials.

Corrected: Murder trials are heard in the Supreme Court.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: In the adversarial system the judge acts as an impartial umpire.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The executive is the arm of government that makes laws.

Corrected: The legislature (parliament) makes laws; the executive carries them out.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Residual powers belong to the states.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Most referendums in Australia have succeeded.

Corrected: Only 8 of 45 referendum proposals have succeeded.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Customary Lore connects people, Country, cultural practice and kinship.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Customary Lore is written in a single code.

Corrected: Customary Lore is an oral tradition and differs between nations.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A state must ratify a treaty before it is bound by it.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The United Nations can force any state to obey international law.

Corrected: International law relies largely on the consent and cooperation of states.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Rights in Australia are protected by the Constitution, statute law, common law and international law.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Rights come without responsibilities.

Corrected: Rights are matched by responsibilities, such as respecting the rights of others.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A person on remand has not been convicted of the offence they are charged with.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Police discretion means police can act outside the law.

Corrected: Police discretion must be used within limits set by legislation and guidelines.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: An accused can apply for a trial by judge alone in NSW.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Legal aid is available to everyone charged with any offence.

Corrected: Legal aid is subject to means, merit and jurisdiction tests.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A partial defence to murder reduces the offence to manslaughter.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Diversionary programs aim to address the causes of offending.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Parole means the sentence has ended.

Corrected: Parole is served in the community as part of the sentence.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The State Parole Authority can revoke parole if conditions are breached.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A continuing detention order is made by the police.

Corrected: A continuing detention order is made by the Supreme Court.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: A victim impact statement can be considered when an offender is sentenced.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The United Nations was founded in 1945.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples is a binding treaty.

Corrected: It is a declaration and is not legally binding.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Nation-states are bound by a treaty only when they consent to it.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: International courts have their own police to arrest suspects.

Corrected: International courts rely on states to arrest and surrender suspects.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Environmental rights and peace rights are categories of human rights.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Forced marriage is a criminal offence in Australia.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: A de facto couple must register their relationship before the law recognises it.

Corrected: Registration is optional; the law looks at the circumstances of the relationship.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: The best interests of the child are protected by both Australian law and the Convention on the Rights of the Child.

items.name: True or false
items.html:
False: Native title can be bought and sold like freehold land.

Corrected: Native title is a communal right under traditional law and cannot be sold like freehold.

items.name: True or false
items.html: True: Crisis and emergency accommodation is a response to homelessness.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Marriage: In Australian law, the union of two people to the exclusion of all others, voluntarily entered into for life.

items.name: Key term
items.html: De facto relationship: A relationship between two people who live together as a couple on a genuine domestic basis and are not married to each other.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Blended family: A family formed when a couple live together with children from earlier relationships.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Kinship: The system of family relationships and obligations that connects Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people to each other, to community and to Country.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Void marriage: A marriage that has no legal effect, for example because one person was already married or did not give real consent.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Parental responsibility: All the duties, powers, responsibilities and authority that parents have by law in relation to their children.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Best interests of the child: The paramount consideration a court must apply when it makes a parenting order.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Adoption: The legal process that permanently transfers parental rights and responsibilities from the birth parents to the adoptive parents.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Parenting plan: A written, signed and dated agreement between parents about the care of their children. It is not enforceable by a court.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Parenting order: A court order about who a child lives with, spends time with and communicates with, and who makes major decisions.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Child support: Money paid by a parent towards the cost of raising a child after separation.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Divorce: The legal ending of a marriage by a court order.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Irretrievable breakdown: The only ground for divorce in Australia, shown by 12 months of separation.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Property settlement: The division of the assets and debts of a couple after separation.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Binding financial agreement: A written agreement between partners, made with independent legal advice, about how property will be divided if they separate.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Apprehended domestic violence order: A court order that restricts a person's behaviour to protect someone they have a domestic relationship with.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Family dispute resolution: A process in which an independent practitioner helps separating families to agree, usually required before applying for a parenting order.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Coercive control: A pattern of abusive behaviour used to control or dominate an intimate partner.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Surrogacy: An arrangement in which a woman agrees to carry a child for another person or couple who will become the child's parents.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Altruistic surrogacy: Surrogacy in which the birth mother receives no payment beyond her reasonable costs.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Parentage order: A court order that transfers legal parentage of a child from the birth mother to the intended parents after surrogacy.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Mandatory reporting: The legal duty of certain workers, such as teachers and doctors, to report a child at risk of significant harm.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Out-of-home care: Care for a child who cannot live safely at home, such as foster care or kinship care.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Human rights: Basic rights and freedoms that belong to every person because they are human. They are universal, inherent, inalienable and indivisible.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Inalienable: Describes rights that cannot be taken or given away.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Universal suffrage: The right of all adult citizens to vote, whatever their sex, race or wealth.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Self-determination: The right of a people to decide their own political status and to pursue their own economic, social and cultural development.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Collective rights: Rights held by a group of people rather than by one person, such as self-determination, environmental rights and peace rights.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Trade union: An organisation of workers formed to protect and improve pay and conditions.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Universal Declaration of Human Rights: The 1948 declaration of the United Nations General Assembly that first set out the rights all people should have. It is not a binding treaty.

items.name: Key term
items.html: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights: The 1966 treaty that binds states to protect rights such as life, liberty, a fair trial, free speech and the vote.

items.name: Key term
items.html: International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights: The 1966 treaty that binds states to work towards rights such as work, health, education and an adequate standard of living.

items.name: Key term
items.html: International Bill of Human Rights: The name given to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the two 1966 covenants together.

items.name: Key term
items.html: State sovereignty: The authority of a state to govern itself and make its own laws without outside interference.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Treaty: A written agreement between states that is binding in international law on the states that ratify it.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Ratification: The step by which a state formally agrees to be bound by a treaty.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Intergovernmental organisation: An organisation whose members are states, set up by treaty, such as the United Nations or the Commonwealth of Nations.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Security Council: The United Nations body responsible for international peace and security. Its five permanent members each hold a veto.

items.name: Key term
items.html: International Court of Justice: The main court of the United Nations. It hears disputes between states and gives advisory opinions.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Human Rights Council: The United Nations body of 47 member states that reviews the human rights record of every member state.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Dualist system: A legal system in which a treaty has no effect in domestic law until parliament passes legislation to enact it.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Express rights: Rights written into the Australian Constitution, such as freedom of religion in s 116.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Implied rights: Rights that the High Court has found are implied by the text and structure of the Constitution, such as the freedom of political communication.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Charter of Rights: A document that lists the rights a government must respect. Australia has none at the national level.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Australian Human Rights Commission: The independent national body that investigates and conciliates complaints of discrimination and breaches of human rights, and reports to parliament.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Shelter: A place to live that gives protection, privacy and security.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Adequate housing: Housing that is secure, affordable, habitable, accessible and in a suitable location, as described in international law.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Social housing: Rental housing provided by the government or community organisations for people on low incomes.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Boarding house: Premises where residents rent a room, not the whole dwelling, and share facilities.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Strata title: Ownership of a unit or lot in a building, together with a share in the common property.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Torrens title: The system in which the government keeps a register of land ownership and guarantees the title shown on it.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Private treaty: The sale of a property at a price negotiated between the seller and the buyer.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Auction: A public sale in which the property is sold to the highest bidder, with no cooling-off period.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Cooling-off period: A short time after contracts are exchanged in which a buyer can withdraw from a private treaty sale.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Mortgage: A loan secured over land. The lender can sell the property if the borrower defaults.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Caveat emptor: "Let the buyer beware": the buyer is responsible for checking the property before buying.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Conveyancing: The legal work of transferring ownership of land from the seller to the buyer.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Exchange of contracts: The point at which the buyer and the seller swap signed contracts and the sale becomes binding.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Residential tenancy agreement: A lease: a contract in which a landlord lets a tenant live in a property in return for rent.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Rental bond: Money paid by a tenant at the start of a lease as security, lodged with NSW Fair Trading.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Condition report: A record of the state of a rented property at the start of a tenancy.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Termination notice: A written notice from a landlord or a tenant that ends a tenancy on a stated date.

items.name: Key term
items.html: NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal: The tribunal that hears most tenancy, strata and home building disputes in NSW.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Security of tenure: A tenant's confidence that they can stay in their home as long as they meet their obligations.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Housing affordability: The relationship between housing costs and household income.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Housing stress: Often defined as a lower-income household spending more than 30 per cent of its income on housing.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Homelessness: Having no home, or living in housing that is inadequate, insecure or without control over one's own space.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Crisis accommodation: Short-term emergency housing for people who have nowhere safe to stay.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Law reform: The process of changing the law so that it better meets the needs and values of society.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Law reform commission: An independent body that reviews areas of law and recommends changes to the government.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Royal commission: A major public inquiry, set up by the government, with strong powers to gather evidence.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Advocacy group: An organisation that campaigns to influence public opinion and the law on an issue.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Repeal: The removal of a law by parliament.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Amendment: A change made to an existing law or to a bill.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Statutory interpretation: The process by which courts work out the meaning of the words in an Act.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Terra nullius: "Land belonging to no one": the doctrine, rejected in 1992, that Australia had no owners before British settlement.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Native title: The recognition in Australian law of the rights and interests of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples in land and waters under their traditional laws and customs.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Land rights: Rights to land granted to Aboriginal people by legislation, such as the Aboriginal Land Rights Act 1983 (NSW).

items.name: Key term
items.html: Aboriginal Land Council: A body set up under NSW legislation that can claim certain Crown land and manage it for Aboriginal people.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Extinguishment: The ending of native title, for example by a grant of freehold land.

items.name: Key term
items.html: eSafety Commissioner: Australia's independent regulator for online safety.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Age assurance: Methods used to check or estimate the age of a person using an online service.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Age-restricted social media platform: A social media service that Australian law requires to take reasonable steps to stop people under 16 from holding accounts.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Prosecution: The party that brings a criminal case against an accused person on behalf of the state.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Accused: A person charged with a criminal offence.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Presumption of innocence: The principle that an accused person is treated as innocent until proved guilty.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Beyond reasonable doubt: The standard of proof in a criminal case.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Summary offence: A less serious offence heard by a magistrate in the Local Court.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Indictable offence: A serious offence usually tried by a judge and jury.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Sanction: A penalty imposed by a court on a person found guilty of an offence.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Plaintiff: The person who starts a civil case.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Defendant: In a civil case, the person who is being sued.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Balance of probabilities: The standard of proof in a civil case: more likely than not.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Tort: A civil wrong, other than a breach of contract, for which the law provides a remedy.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Negligence: A failure to take reasonable care that causes harm to a person to whom a duty of care is owed.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Duty of care: A legal obligation to avoid acts or omissions that could reasonably be foreseen to harm others.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Contract: A legally binding agreement between two or more parties.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Damages: Money awarded by a court to compensate a plaintiff for loss.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Injunction: A court order that requires a person to do, or to stop doing, something.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Administrative law: The area of law that deals with the decisions and actions of government bodies and officials.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Judicial review: A court's review of whether a government decision was made lawfully.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Merits review: A fresh look at a government decision by a tribunal, which can change the decision.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Tribunal: A body that resolves certain disputes with less cost and formality than a court.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Ombudsman: An independent official who investigates complaints about government agencies.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Alternative dispute resolution: Ways of settling a dispute without a court hearing, such as negotiation, mediation and conciliation.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Mediation: A process in which a neutral third person helps the parties reach their own agreement.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Evolving capacity: The idea that children gain the ability to make their own decisions as they mature.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Age of criminal responsibility: The age below which a child cannot be charged with a criminal offence: 10 in NSW.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Doli incapax: The presumption that a child aged 10 to under 14 does not know that their conduct is seriously wrong.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Recidivism: Reoffending after being dealt with by the criminal justice system.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Diversion: Dealing with an offender, especially a young person, outside the formal court process.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Youth justice conference: A meeting in which a young offender, the victim and others agree on a plan to repair the harm.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Convention on the Rights of the Child: The 1989 treaty that sets out the rights of everyone under 18.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Asylum seeker: A person who has left their country and applied for protection as a refugee, and whose claim has not yet been decided.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Refugee: A person outside their country who has a well-founded fear of persecution because of their race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership of a particular social group.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Non-refoulement: The duty not to return a person to a place where they face persecution or serious harm.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Mandatory detention: The legal requirement that a non-citizen in Australia without a valid visa be detained.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Offshore processing: The assessment of asylum claims in a country other than the one where protection is sought.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Protection visa: A visa granted to a person in Australia who is found to be owed protection.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Law: A set of rules made by the state that binds everyone in the community and is enforced by the courts.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Rule of law: The principle that everyone, including the government, is subject to the law and equal before it.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Justice: The fair and impartial treatment of all people under the law.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Procedural fairness: The right to a fair hearing by an unbiased decision-maker.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Public law: Law that governs the relationship between individuals and the state, such as criminal and constitutional law.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Private law: Law that governs relationships between individuals, such as contract and tort law.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Anarchy: The absence of law and government.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Common law: Law made by judges through their decisions in cases.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Statute law: Law made by parliament.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Precedent: A court decision that guides or binds later courts deciding similar cases.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Ratio decidendi: The legal reason for a court's decision, which forms the binding precedent.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Obiter dicta: Remarks made by a judge in passing that are not binding but may be persuasive.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Stare decisis: The principle that courts stand by what has already been decided.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Bill: A proposed law that has not yet been passed by parliament.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Royal assent: The formal approval of a bill by the Governor-General or a Governor, which makes it an Act.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Delegated legislation: Rules made by a body that parliament has given the power to make them, such as regulations and by-laws.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Jurisdiction: The power of a court to hear a particular kind of matter.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Original jurisdiction: The power of a court to hear a case for the first time.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Appellate jurisdiction: The power of a court to hear appeals from lower courts.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Adversarial system: A system of trial in which two opposing sides present their cases to an impartial judge or jury.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Division of powers: The way the Constitution shares law-making power between the Commonwealth and the states.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Separation of powers: The division of government into the legislature, the executive and the judiciary so that no one body holds all power.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Exclusive powers: Law-making powers that only the Commonwealth Parliament can use.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Concurrent powers: Law-making powers shared by the Commonwealth and the states.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Residual powers: Law-making powers left with the states because the Constitution does not give them to the Commonwealth.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Referendum: A national vote on a proposal to change the Constitution.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Customary Lore: The laws, customs and practices of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, passed on by word of mouth, story, song and ceremony.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Elder: A respected senior member of an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander community who holds and passes on knowledge and Lore.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Country: The lands, waters and skies to which Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples are connected.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Customary international law: Rules that bind states because states follow them consistently out of a sense of legal duty.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Nation-state: A political unit with a defined territory, a permanent population, a government and the capacity to deal with other states.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Remand: Being held in custody while waiting for a trial or sentence.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Judge-alone trial: A trial for an indictable offence in which a judge, without a jury, decides the verdict.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Diversionary program: A program that directs an offender away from the usual court or prison path and into treatment, education or support.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Security classification: The level of security, such as maximum, medium or minimum, at which a prisoner is held.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Extended supervision order: A Supreme Court order that keeps a high-risk offender under strict supervision in the community after their sentence ends.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Continuing detention order: A Supreme Court order that keeps a high-risk offender in custody after their sentence ends.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Non-parole period: The minimum time an offender must spend in custody before being eligible for release on parole.

items.name: Key term
items.html: International relations: The ways nation-states and international organisations deal with each other, including through diplomacy, trade, law and conflict.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Diplomacy: The management of relations between states by negotiation.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Multilateral treaty: A treaty between three or more states.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Bilateral treaty: A treaty between two states.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Globalisation: The growing connection of countries through trade, technology, travel and communication.

items.name: Key term
items.html: United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples: The 2007 declaration that sets out the individual and collective rights of Indigenous peoples. It is not a binding treaty.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Forced marriage: A marriage entered into without the free and full consent of one or both people, because of coercion, threat or deception, or where a person is under 16.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Foster care: Care of a child in the home of an authorised carer when the child cannot live safely with their parents.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Child Placement Principle: The principle that an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander child who cannot live at home should be placed, in order of priority, with family, community or other Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander carers.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Real property: Land and anything fixed to it, such as a house.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Community housing: Social housing managed by not-for-profit organisations.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Public housing: Social housing owned and managed by the state government.

items.name: Key term
items.html: Specialist homelessness service: A funded service that gives accommodation and support to people who are homeless or at risk of homelessness.
